entries.title: Bears' Caleb Williams, Bulls players lead PCA cheering section
entries.summary: <p>Sitting in the front row behind the Cubs dugout, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears quarterback Caleb Williams</a> donned a Pete Crow-Armstrong jersey and led cheers for his MVP candidacy.</p><p>Joining him were Caleb Wilson, the No. 4 pick in this year’s draft, and fellow Bull Matas Buzelis, who is one of Williams’ friends. Cole Bennett, aka video director Lyrical Lemonade, joined them.</p><p>The Cubs posted a social media video of the three banging on the dugout roof and leading the crowd in a “PCA” cheer until Crow-Armstrong turned around the wave at them.</p><p>Williams said on Thursday’s edition of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/03/bears-caleb-williams-hot-ones-debut-top-5-moments-ben-johnson-quarterback-nfl-hot-wings" target="_blank" >“Hot Ones”</a> that he considered Buzelis, Crow-Armstrong and Bennett among the friends that have helped him love Chicago.</p><p>They weren’t the only stars at Wrigley Field for the Cubs-Brewers game — Pacers point guard Tyrese Haliburton threw out the ceremonial first pitch.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="und" dir="ltr">W. <a href="https://t.co/tbN2esUnVE">pic.twitter.com/tbN2esUnVE</a></p>— Chicago Cubs (@Cubs) <a href="https://x.com/Cubs/status/2095686099737702886?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 4, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Williams, who recently shaved his beard into a mustache, showed it off on the videoboard.</p><p>Teammate Kalif Raymond joked earlier Thursday that the “camp ‘stache” made Williams looked like his dad, Carl.</p><p>“I mean, he looks like he got four kids on the way right now,” he said, laughing.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">are they really your friends if they don't ride for you like this? <a href="https://t.co/wEHBxNIEho">pic.twitter.com/wEHBxNIEho</a></p>— Chicago Cubs (@Cubs) <a href="https://x.com/Cubs/status/2095684452877750511?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 4, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Crow-Armstrong had a homer and two RBIs in a 2-1 win.</p><p>The Bears began for a three-day break after Thursday's practice.</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Pete Crow-Armstrong fuels Cubs win in front of fellow sports stars: ‘Chicago’s got a lot to look forward to’
entries.summary: <p>Every game he plays at Wrigley Field, <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b> has a cheering section nearly 40,000 strong.</p><p>But a few members of Thursday night’s Wrigley Field crowd stood out, adding some juice not only to the stadium-wide party but for the Cubs’ MVP candidate, specifically.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong did his thing, homering in the third inning to drive in the Cubs’ only runs in a 2-1 win that earned a series split with the rival Brewers.</p><p>He did it in front of Bears quarterback <b>Caleb Williams</b> and Bulls players <b>Matas Buzelis</b> and <b>Caleb Wilson</b>, the current generation of Chicago sports stars gathering in the thick of the Cubs’ pennant race.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Official meeting of the PCA fan club. 🤝 <a href="https://t.co/5ZBP2q2jMz">pic.twitter.com/5ZBP2q2jMz</a></p>— Chicago Cubs (@Cubs) <a href="https://x.com/Cubs/status/2095669954775224581?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 4, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>“Those are good people, those are my people,” Crow-Armstrong said. “Those are great representatives of Chicago.</p><p>“It was awesome having them here. I felt the energy from the crowd when they got put on the [video] board. Chicago’s got a lot to look forward to with those three.”</p><p>Crow-Armstrong didn’t include himself in what Chicago has to look forward to, though he certainly belongs at the forefront of that conversation, putting up a ridiculous campaign that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/29/cubs-star-pete-crow-armstrong-hits-three-home-runs-to-bolster-mvp-case" >has him favored to win the NL MVP</a>.</p><p>His home run Thursday was his 39th of the year, putting him one away from becoming the 10th Cub ever to smack 40 bombs in a single season.</p><p>All that individual stuff isn’t Crow-Armstrong’s thing, though.</p><p>Earlier in the day, he was named the NL Player of the Month after an outrageously productive August. Asked what it meant to earn that honor for the second time this season, Crow-Armstrong was blunt.</p><p>“Nothing,” he said.</p><p>His focus on the team has been consistent throughout the year, and delivering a win Thursday night certainly meant a lot more than nothing.</p><p>Doing it in front of his fellow Chicago sports icons-in-the-making meant something, too.</p><p>“It’s huge having guys show up and support each other,” Crow-Armstrong said. “Just the friendship alone is great, and I’m lucky to have that. But to be able to show the city that we’re all pulling for each other and we all believe in each other is huge.”</p><p>Oh, the city loved it.</p><p>As Crow-Armstrong mentioned, Williams and the two Bulls were shown on the video board, with the camera panning to Crow-Armstrong, who pointed at them from the dugout.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">are they really your friends if they don't ride for you like this? <a href="https://t.co/wEHBxNIEho">pic.twitter.com/wEHBxNIEho</a></p>— Chicago Cubs (@Cubs) <a href="https://x.com/Cubs/status/2095684452877750511?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 4, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>The crowd went wild and started what’s been a frequent outburst this summer at Wrigley – predictable after Williams’ playoff heroics – chanting, “GREEN BAY SUCKS!”</p><p>Asked after the game if that was truly the case, Crow-Armstrong chuckled and said, “Historically? No.</p><p>“You’ll have to ask the masses on that one. They’d have a different answer, I think.”</p><p><b>Gausman’s gem</b></p><p>Righty starter <b>Kevin Gausman</b> was once more excellent on Thursday, throwing seven innings of one-run ball against the Brewers, allowing just five hits.</p><p>Though he’s gone back and forth between terrific outings like Thursday’s and less impressive ones, Gausman has mostly been exactly what the Cubs thought he’d be when they brought him in on a deadline deal to pitch at the top of their starting rotation.</p><p>“That’s all you want from someone you pick up at the deadline,” Crow-Armstrong said. “Gaus was absolutely dominant.”</p><p><b>Bullpen better</b></p><p>In the middle of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/02/cubs-bullpen-relief-pitchers-stats-daniel-palencia-jacob-webb-trent-thornton-justin-steele-javier-assad-edward-cabrera-pedro-ramirez" >a bout of bullpen blues</a>, Cubs relievers <b>Ryan Zeferjahn</b> and <b>Ryan Rolison</b> were perfect in the eighth and ninth innings Thursday, preserving a one-run lead.</p><p>“We need some good outings from our bullpen,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said. “They were both excellent today. Obviously, you come into a one-run game in the eighth inning, you come into a one-run game in the ninth inning, those are tough innings.”</p>

entries.title: 37-year-old man fatally shot in South Shore area
entries.summary: <p>A man was fatally wounded in a shooting in South Shore Thursday evening, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, 37, was in front of a business in the 7300 block of South Stony Island Avenue at 6:04 p.m. when a woman reportedly fired shots at the location, police said. </p><p>The unidentified victim was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center, where he later died.</p><p>Police are investigating the incident, and no one is currently in custody.</p>

entries.title: 2 more belugas die at Shedd Aquarium
entries.summary: <p>Three beluga whales have died of unclear causes at the Shedd Aquarium in the past several days, just weeks after the institution received several rescued whales.</p><p>The two most recent beluga deaths occurred Wednesday, the aquarium said.</p><p>One whale, a 20-year-old female named Rain, had been rescued weeks earlier from a shuttered Canadian aquatic park where dozens of whales were living under allegedly poor conditions. The other, 34-year-old Beethoven, was part of Shedd’s resident beluga pod.</p><p>It's unclear if their deaths were related, the Shedd said in a statement Thursday morning, about a week after another rescued beluga, Peekachu, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/08/26/one-of-the-shedds-rescued-beluga-whales-has-died" >also died of unknown causes</a> on Aug. 25. </p><p>"These losses are hard, made more difficult by the fact that it will take time to get concrete answers about what led to their passings," the Shedd said in the statement.</p><p>The aquarium said it will perform tests to learn more about why the belugas died.</p><p>"Some answers may come quickly, while others may take more time to come into focus. Given how closely the public has followed the rescue effort, Shedd felt it was important to share this news now rather than wait for every answer," the statement reads.</p><p>Shedd had a similar response last week, after Peekachu’s death, noting at the time that the whale was not “consistently eating her full diet. When we looked at the blood values, we were concerned that she was dehydrated and needed supportive care.”</p><p>A cause of death for Peekachu had not been released as of Thursday.</p><p>Shedd is part of a consortium of four U.S. and one Spanish aquarium that together agreed to take 30 belugas languishing in Marineland, located in Niagara Falls, Canada. Marineland had faced criticism for years that its animals were living in unsanitary conditions. </p><p>The park closed to the public in 2024, and Marineland officials, citing extreme financial difficulties, had threatened to euthanize the whales if permanent homes couldn’t be found.</p><p>Shedd received 10 Marineland belugas, more than doubling their resident population.</p><p>The Marineland belugas "had nowhere else to go," the Shedd said in its statement. "Shedd and accredited partners were asked to step in. Helping these animals in need is part of Shedd’s responsibility, and our commitment to these whales and their second chance remains unchanged. We appreciate the outpouring of support from so many others who are equally committed to animal welfare."</p><p>Animal rights activists, while relieved that the whales are no longer at Marineland, have expressed concerns that the rescued belugas might be bred — leading to more cetaceans living in captivity. They’ve also said the Marineland belugas are likely sick and transporting them in trucks and airplanes could make them more so.</p><p>“The deaths of Peekachu and Rain bring up very serious questions about their health status prior to being transferred to Shedd and the judgement used in that decision,” said Lori Marino, co-founder and president of the planned Whale Sanctuary Project in Port Hilford Bay, Nova Scotia. “There has been no transparency on this issue from Marineland, and we need to know who made the decision to move these animals now and why. The death of Beethoven is very concerning because he was already at Shedd. So there have been three sudden unexplained deaths within one week at Shedd. This leaves open the possibility that either the deaths were caused by stress or some kind of pathogen or both.”</p><p>Andrew Burns, a longtime adviser and lawyer for Marineland, told the Sun-Times Thursday that “We have absolute faith in Shedd’s abilities and reputation to do everything possible” for the Marineland belugas.</p><p>Burns, asked about the health of the whales that ended up at Shedd, said: “I don’t have details on individual records of whale health. All whales were fit to transport and certificates were provided.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-history/2026/08/07/beluga-whale-shedd-aquarium-abbott-oceanarium" target="_blank" >When Shedd Aquarium’s first beluga whales came to Chicago</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/08/12/shedd-aquarium-to-receive-four-more-beluga-whales-from-marineland" >Shedd Aquarium to receive four more beluga whales from Marineland</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/07/22/belugas-chicago-shedd-aquarium-marineland-canada-rescue" target="_blank" >Rescued belugas have arrived in Chicago. The move is unprecedented — and controversial</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/animals/2026/07/23/first-look-belugas-shedd-aquarium-whales-canada-trip" target="_blank" >First look at Shedd Aquarium’s newest beluga whales: Acadia, Lillooet, Osiris, Sierra</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/museums-zoos/2026/08/26/one-of-the-shedds-rescued-beluga-whales-has-died" >One of the Shedd’s rescued beluga whales has died</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Illinois opens season with 42-23 victory against visiting UAB
entries.summary: <p>CHAMPAIGN — Katin Houser threw three touchdown passes and ran for a score in his Illinois debut as the Illini defeated UAB 42-23 on Thursday night in a season opener.</p><p>Houser, who transferred from East Carolina, completed 13 of 17 passes for 182 yards. Collin Dixon caught six passes for 70 yards and two TDs, and Ca’Lil Valentine rushed 11 times for 88 yards and a score.</p><p>UAB's Ryder Burton completed 18 of 33 passes for 219 yards and a TD. He also rushed for a score. Jonah Delange kicked three field goals for the Blazers.</p><p>Illinois scored two TDs on its first six plays and led 21-13 at halftime.</p><p>A 65-yard punt return by Mac Resetich set up the first TD — an 18-yard pass from Houser to Dixon. Valentine scored on a 51-yard run.</p><p>The Illini scored on the final play of the half, a 54-yard “Hail Mary” pass from Houser to Ty Robinson, who caught the ball after it was bobbled in the end zone by a UAB player.</p><p>It was the first successful “Hail Mary” by Illinois in seven years.</p><p><b>The takeaway</b></p><p>It was difficult to judge the success of Illinois’ new 3-5-5 defense, brought to Champaign by new defensive coordinator Bobby Hauck.</p><p>The Illini were hurt by several missed tackles, not a lack of familiarity of the new scheme.</p><p>Despite the 19-point loss, UAB didn’t look like a team that went 4-8 a year ago, fired head coach Trent Dilfer at midseason after the Super Bowl-winning QB had lost 21 of 30 games in two-plus seasons, and finally ended a four-year, 42-game road losing streak in its final game last season.</p><p>The Blazers outgained Illinois 413-333 and if wasn’t for the pass at the end of the first half that changed the game's momentum, would have made Illinois sweat a little more on the warm, muggy night.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>Illinois: Hosts Duke on Sept. 12.</p><p>UAB: Hosts Louisiana-Monroe on Sept. 12.</p>

entries.title: Corliss dominates Brooks, hopes to ride strong junior leadership back to the state playoffs
entries.summary: <p>Coach Keith Brookshire has been steadily building at Corliss. Last year, the team picked up a first-round Class 5A state playoff win. That victory made an impression on several sophomores who were starting on varsity.</p><p>Two of them, linemen Demitris Loggers and Jaquan Gumm, have developed program-changing personalities as juniors.</p><p>“This is the most leadership we have had,” Brookshire said. “Loggers and Gumm are the main guys. I’ve seen great growth from them over the offseason, and they are doing a great job keeping everyone in line. This is the first year I’ve had that. Guys are doing what they are supposed to do.”</p><p>Loggers and Gumm also provided the blocking for some major offensive fireworks in the Trojans’ 52-12 win over host Brooks on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/09/03/high-school-football-scores-chicago-illinois" >Thursday</a>.</p><p>Senior quarterback Jayce Trigg connected with senior Jaylin Moore for a 58-yard touchdown in the second minute of the game.</p><p>“It felt great,” Trigg said. “There were nothing but openings, and he took them. Once we connect, it is over with. That is our bond on the field.”</p><p>Trigg was 6 of 11 passing for 174 yards with two touchdowns and no interceptions. He also had seven carries for 154 yards and two touchdowns. His 69-yard TD run midway through the third quarter put Corliss (2-1) ahead 32-6.</p><p>Moore, who also plays safety, caught three passes for 89 yards and hauled in an interception in the fourth quarter.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-d70000" name="html-embed-module-d70000"></a><blockquote class="tiktok-embed" cite="https://www.tiktok.com/@michaelsobriensports/video/7681510324696010014" data-video-id="7681510324696010014" style="max-width: 605px;min-width: 325px;" > <section> <a target="_blank" title="@michaelsobriensports" href="https://www.tiktok.com/@michaelsobriensports?refer=embed">@michaelsobriensports</a> Corliss beat Brooks 52-12. entries.title: Enes Kanter Freedom sues the Sky after being ejected from game
entries.summary: <p>Former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom is suing the Sky after being <a class="Link" href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/wnba/2026/08/23/enes-kanter-freedom-ejected-wnba-game-natasha-cloud/91436373007/" target="_blank" >ejected during a game against the Indiana Fever</a> last month and receiving <a class="Link" href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/wnba/2026/08/25/enes-kanter-freedom-ban-chicago-sky/91464324007/" target="_blank" >an indefinite ban from attending games at Wintrust Arena</a>.</p><p>Kanter Freedom filed a lawsuit against the Sky in the U.S District Court for the Northern District of Illinois on Thursday, according to court documents obtained by Fox News. Kanter Freedom named Chicago Women’s Basketball Operations, LLC, which operates the Sky, the Metropolitan Pier and Exposition Authority (MPEA), the corporation that owns Wintrust Arena, and the City of Chicago as defendants.</p><p>Emails seeking comment from the Sky and WNBA were not immediately returned.</p><p>The complaint says Kanter Freedom's First Amendment rights were violated when he was "wrongfully ejected" from the Aug. 23 game in Chicago. It frames Kanter Freedom as the "target of a torrent of hateful attacks and discriminatory actions based on (his) viewpoint and gender identity."</p><p>"The Chicago Sky; MPEA, through Wintrust Arena Security; and the City of Chicago, by its Police Department, worked together to eject (Kanter Freedom) in retaliation for protected expressions, and continue to work together to enforce the ongoing, unconstitutional ban of Plaintiff from Wintrust Arena," the lawsuit said.</p><p>Kanter Freedom was sitting courtside when he entered into a shouting match with Sky guard Natasha Cloud with 1:22 to go in the third quarter. Cloud approached Kanter Freedom, who stood up, stepped onto the court and past photographers with his arms outstretched before security intervened.</p><p>As Kanter Freedom was escorted out of the arena, he pointed to his shirt that read, "WOMAN noun. adult human female." The incident reignited tense discourse around transgender participation in the league, which <a class="Link" href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/wnba/2026/08/24/enes-kanter-wnba-draft-eligibility-royce-white/91446929007/" target="_blank" >Kanter Freedom inserted himself into by declaring for the 2027 WNBA Draft</a> last month.</p><p>Two days later,<a class="Link" href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/wnba/2026/08/25/enes-kanter-freedom-ban-chicago-sky/91464324007/" target="_blank" > Sky owner Michael Alter announced that Kanter Freedom has been barred</a> from entering Wintrust Arena, stating Kanter Freedom was attempting to "provoke" Cloud to further his own agenda.</p><p>“It was pretty clear to us that his purpose of coming here was trying to be provocative and just see how much attention he could get,” Alter said Aug. 25. "He portrays as this victimless person who did nothing, said nothing. Just wearing a T-shirt. ... We have five different security authorities that all agreed very quickly to throw him out because he made himself into a threat."</p><p>Alter said Kanter Freedom's ban will remain in place until he can "prove to us that he's able to abide by our rules without being a potential threat."</p><p>According to the Sky's Fan Code of Conduct — which applies to all ticket holders — the Sky and Wintrust Arena reserve the right to "eject any patron that poses a threat to themselves or other guests. This includes, but not limited to, profanity, racial or ethnic comments, intoxication, disorderly conduct, drug use, sexual harassment, or other intimidating actions directed at officials, players, coaches, spectators, or team representatives. These will not be tolerated and are grounds for dismissal from the arena at the ticket holders expense."</p><p>The lawsuit said Kanter Freedom "poses absolutely no danger or immediate threat to public safety."</p><h2>What Enes Kanter Freedom said about lawsuit</h2><p>Kanter Freedom shared the first page of his lawsuit on X on Thursday, writing, "I’m taking legal action over my ejection from the @chicagosky game while peacefully exercising my First Amendment rights."</p><p>He added, "My T-shirt did what the whole @WNBA apparently couldn’t: define a woman. No threats. No violence. Just biology. And somehow, that required a security escort. You don’t have to agree with my speech but you don’t get to silence me for it. I will not be intimidated. I will not be silenced. I will continue to stand for women and defend free speech."</p><p>A transgender woman has never played in the WNBA, but the league has become a lightning rod for the topic after comments made by <a class="Link" href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/basketball/wnba/fever/2026/08/19/sophie-cunningham-wnba-culture-war-transgender/91370570007/" target="_blank" >Fever guard Sophie Cunningham</a> were published in <a class="Link" href="https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/wnba/2026/07/22/sophie-cunningham-trans-participation-espn/91008075007/" target="_blank" >an ESPN story</a><a class="Link" href="https://go.skimresources.com/?id=83224X1595658&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.espn.com%2Fwnba%2Fstory%2F_%2Fid%2F49306657%2Fsophie-cunningham-finger-point-indiana-fever-wnba&xcust=SC1-USAT_u56OQoxsmE3JqMBN2_u5mPOYAlYA237mJNZQb3MiZ&sref=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.usatoday.com%2Fstory%2Fsports%2Fwnba%2F2026%2F08%2F24%2Fenes-kanter-wnba-draft-eligibility-royce-white%2F91446929007%2F" target="_blank" > on July 21</a>. Cunningham <a class="Link" href="https://www.usatoday.com/videos/sports/basketball/wnba/fever/2026/07/22/sophie-cunningham-doubles-down-on-transgender-comment-protecting-girls-sports/91017055007/" target="_blank" >then doubled down</a>, saying young girls playing sports "shouldn't have to go against biological men."</p><p>Legislation passed in 27 states barring transgender girls and women from participating in women's sports is aimed at a small portion of the population — 1% of people aged 13 and over in the U.S. identify as transgender, according to <a class="Link" href="https://williamsinstitute.law.ucla.edu/publications/trans-adults-united-states/" target="_blank" >a 2025 study by the Williams Institute</a> at UCLA Law.</p><p>The Human Rights Campaign reported in 2023 that 19% of transgender youth nationwide were playing sports, including <a class="Link" href="https://hrc-prod-requests.s3-us-west-2.amazonaws.com/YouthReport_2023_Tables_080923.pdf" target="_blank" >fewer than 1,300 who played sports in school</a>.</p><p>Kanter Freedom was selected third overall by the <a class="Link" href="https://sportsdata.usatoday.com/basketball/nba/teams/utah-jazz/26/" target="_blank" >Utah Jazz</a> in the 2011 NBA draft and went on to play 11 seasons, where he averaged 11.2 points and 7.8 rebounds across 748 regular-season games. He played four seasons in Utah, followed by stints in Oklahoma, New York, Portland and Boston.<br></p>

entries.title: Tony Romo vs. CBS might be best game this NFL season that no one sees
entries.summary: <p>We’re less than a week away from the NFL season opener, and we have no idea whether CBS will put analyst Tony Romo, the pride and joy of Eastern Illinois, back on the air.</p><p>A decision doesn’t figure to come anytime soon after Romo pleaded no contest Tuesday to a charge of operating while intoxicated and issued a statement in which he apologized and revealed his struggles with pain medication and alcohol.</p><p>“As I turn my attention to my health, my family and, in time, my return to CBS, I kindly ask for privacy during this period,” Romo said.</p><p>Romo’s return to CBS seems unlikely but not out of the question. The most likely outcome is a settlement that rids CBS of Romo’s albatross of a contract — reportedly $18 million per year with four years left — and removes the stain he has become on its image.</p><p>And not just because of his arrest and embarrassing body-camera footage.</p><p>CBS put Romo, who was stopped by police just up the road on Interstate 43 in Wisconsin, on leave and replaced him alongside Jim Nantz on its top crew with JJ Watt. The former star defensive end’s stock skyrocketed in his first season on the No. 2 team with Ian Eagle, and he very well could stay on the top team with another strong performance.</p><p>Romo hadn’t had one of those in years, perhaps not since his first contract — a modest three-year, roughly $9 million deal — during which he took the NFL broadcasting world by storm with predictive powers never seen before. Whether the obscene payday affected his work, we’ll never know, but Romo often appeared unprepared and at times unprofessional since then.</p><p>CBS’ silence on the matter speaks volumes. The network’s last public remarks – other than “No comment” – were Aug. 11, when CBS Sports president David Berson said he had no timeline for a decision on Romo’s future and explained why he put the ex-quarterback on indefinite leave.</p><p>“We had to consider the impact on our image and on our brand,” Berson told reporters at the network’s NFL media day. “That’s very important to us. Whether the games, marketing, PR, social, the focus should and needs to be on our presentation and not on any other factors.”</p><p>Good luck with that.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/09/01/tony-romo-pleads-no-contest-to-operating-while-intoxicated" >Tony Romo pleads no contest to operating while intoxicated</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/08/28/tony-romo-facing-three-more-citations-in-connection-with-his-arrest-cbs-cowboys" >Tony Romo facing three more citations in connection with his arrest</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-media/2026/08/11/tony-romo-cbs-sports-nfl" >No timeline for a decision on Tony Romo’s future, CBS Sports president says</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Meanwhile, Romo’s agents and attorneys will be hard at work trying to either save his job or his money. Romo is represented by the powerful Creative Artists Agency, specifically R.J. Gonser, who negotiated Romo’s monster deal with CBS.</p><p>An agent has three objectives in such a crisis: Keep the client employed (Romo hasn’t been fired), manage the publicity (his statement seeks sympathy) and if neither can be accomplished, negotiate as good of a settlement as possible.</p><p>CBS might have Romo’s contract in its favor to fire him for cause. Standard language explains that cause includes but isn’t limited to “gross misconduct,” “arrest for, charged with, indictment for, plea of guilty to, or conviction of, a felony or of a crime” and “conduct that brings employee or the company into public disrepute, contempt, scandal or ridicule.”</p><p>In his statement, Romo included that he pleaded “no contest to a civil offense for OWI in Wisconsin,” seemingly to address similar contract language. He didn’t commit a criminal offense, and as part of his plea, he had several citations dismissed.</p><p>And by expressing contrition and indicating he has a problem, Romo probably lowered the chances of CBS outright firing him. It could look heartless, no matter how bad Romo’s game analysis has been.</p><p>The question is: Does CBS think what Romo did was bad enough to cut ties, even if only for “public disrepute.” Fortunately, he didn’t hurt anyone. The network certainly could help Romo clean himself up and eventually put him with a lower broadcast crew, or even somewhere else in Paramount’s empire, allowing him to work his way back. But CBS has no obligation to stand by Romo in any way.</p><p>That would contrast with how NBC handled Al Michaels’ arrest for suspicion of drunk driving in April 2013. That September, Michaels was on the call for “Sunday Night Football.” The differences appear to be that Michaels was beloved and he wasn’t making $18 million a year.</p><p>Though CBS wants viewers to focus on the games, in the back of their mind, they’ll wonder what’s happening with Romo. For now, CBS and Romo are playing nicely. But eventually, negotiations will get hot and heavy. The network might point to its morals clause, saying Romo endangered the public and damaged CBS’ reputation. Romo then might threaten to sue.</p><p>It’ll happen in private, but it could make for great TV, probably even better than many of those games.</p><h3>Remote patrol</h3><p><b>Matt Vasgersian</b>, <b>Steve Stone</b> and <b>Justin Morneau</b> will call the Twins-White Sox game for “Sunday Night Baseball,” which will air on NBCSN and Peacock. <b>Ahmed Fareed</b> will host the pregame show with <b>Eric Hosmer</b>, who also will be the “Inside the Pitch” analyst. First pitch is scheduled for 5:20 p.m.</p><p>For the conspiracy theorists in the audience, NBC's lead crew, with former Sox voice <b>Jason Benetti</b>, always was scheduled to call Phillies-Braves at noon. Twins-Sox was flexed into “SNB” for Blue Jays-Royals. It marks the Sox’ first home game on “Sunday Night Baseball” with fans since June 29, 2008, against the Cubs.<br></p>

entries.title: Hegseth needs to go if the GOP expects midterm success
entries.summary: <p>“Muscles, dudes in dresses, testosterone.”</p><p>That’s how one European defense official described the priorities of U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, according to a <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/02/politics/hegseths-army-leadership-void-culture-war?selected=cnn-subs-monthly&source=sub_web_wall-met" target="_blank" >bombshell new report</a> from CNN on the growing concern inside the U.S. military over Hegseth’s leadership.</p><p>Hegseth might not disagree with the characterization. He’s made it his mission to focus his attention on the culture wars, wokeism, diversity, equity and inclusion, and what soldiers look like, and it’s creating “turbulence” inside the military he oversees.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-100000" name="module-100000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>Recent high-profile resignations and firings by Hegseth have also brought increased scrutiny at the Pentagon, with Army Secretary Dan Driscoll abruptly announcing <a class="Link" href="https://www.mediaite.com/media/tv/bret-baier-surprised-by-army-secretarys-abrupt-resignation-thought-he-was-gonna-stay/" target="_blank" >he was leaving</a> this week.</p><p>“You’re taking away three of the most seasoned combat leaders of a generation who are in a unique position to articulate battlefield requirements,” a former Army official said of Hegseth’s “forced exits” of Army chief of staff Randy George; former head of U.S. Army Europe and Africa, Gen. Christopher Donahue; and former commander of U.S. Army transformation and training command, Gen. David Hodne.</p><p>This all comes against the backdrop of what is perceived as an increasingly unwinnable and also unendable Iran war, which is losing support by the day.</p><p>In March, <a class="Link" href="https://www.natesilver.net/p/iran-war-polls-popularity-approval" target="_blank" >opposition</a> to the war was at 47.3%, and now, six months later, it’s at 55.7%.</p><p>None of this is helpful for Republicans who are campaigning in tight and uphill contests all over the country. They are already having to defend President Donald Trump’s tariffs and burgeoning trade war with Canada, his impolitic comments about affordability “hoaxes,” and the sense that his priorities — building ballrooms and hosting UFC fights — are out of whack with voters.</p><p>The never-ending war in Iran is the last thing they want to be talking about.</p><p>Hopes that Trump can effectively wind the war down before the midterms have been whittled down to a nub — prediction markets don’t have peace talks occurring until 2027.</p><p>But he could make a move that improves the politics of this quagmire for him and Republicans in time for elections: Fire Hegseth.</p><p>Hegseth’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/cnn-data-guru-reveals-red-164633153.html" target="_blank" >net approval</a> is at a miserable minus 22 — well below other Trump Cabinet officials, including Health and Human Services Secretary Bobby Kennedy Jr.</p><p>His own commanders are publicly voicing their concerns about his leadership. Reports of critical shortages of missiles and other materials are bringing into question our military’s readiness. And stories of hellish conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, including attempts by multiple sailors to jump overboard, are dogging Hegseth’s tenure. Not to mention earlier scandals over legally questionable drug boat strikes and improper use of Signal chats.</p><p>A change in leadership would have the practical effect of restoring order to the Defense Department, and the political effect of changing the narrative for Trump and Republicans at a crucial time, just two months before midterm elections.</p><p>Hegseth doesn’t want to do this job anyway, it appears. Despite being busy prosecuting a war that’s disrupted the global economy, killed and injured hundreds of U.S. troops and made the region far more dangerous for our allies, he’s been seen on the campaign trail, stumping for candidates in Iowa and Kentucky — explicitly partisan, political moves that other Pentagon leaders have always avoided.</p><p>“We’re restoring the warrior ethos inside our department because that matters. We need guys like this man right here having our back in Congress,” he <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/17/us/politics/hegseth-iowa-campaign-nunn.html" target="_blank" >said</a> of Rep. Zach Nunn, R-Iowa, in August.</p><p>As long as I’ve known him, Pete has wanted to run for president, and he’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2028-election/pete-hegseth-talking-possible-run-president-2028-sources-say-rcna594891" target="_blank" >reportedly</a> said as much to friends and colleagues.</p><p>So Trump should do him, Republicans and all Americans a favor, and cut him loose so he can go back to Fox News and focus on the things that matter to him: muscles, dudes in dresses, and testosterone.</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e90000" name="module-e90000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Bears can stay. Suits can take a hike.
entries.summary: <p>NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/27/bears-stadium-hammond-arlington-heights-commissioner-roger-goodell-opportunity-keep-illinois-nfl" >indicated</a> a preference for keeping a team in Illinois as well as for the league's expansion to Europe.</p><p>All can be accomplished by letting George McCaskey pack his cleats and pads and move to one of his favorite spots around Wolf Lake, Lost Marsh Golf Course or some other desirable landfill in Indiana.</p><p>At the same time, the Saudi financiers of the failing LIV Golf enterprise should be invited to sink a billion or so of their own coin into a dome and a few amenities for Soldier Field. In return, they get an expansion team. The new "pride and joy of Illinois" rises on the city's beautiful lakefront. Mayor Brandon Johnson might even jump in and take some credit. TV networks will drool over buying broadcast rights to the first game featuring the Indiana Bears as visitors.</p><p>At the same time, Bears President Kevin Warren can be packed off to London, Berlin or some other far-flung locale to begin work on a new NFL football palace overseas. Expansion team No. 2 will play there. Costs, of course, will be borne by the European local taxpayers found to be at least as gullible as those of Northern Indiana.</p><p>Everyone wins, and the NFL's future is bright.<br> <br><i>Tom Stall, McHenry</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-730000" name="module-730000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Growling over the Bears </h3><p>Tell Roger Goodell to shut up and stay out of the Bears stadium business. And tell Illinois legislators, again, that taxpayers refuse to foot any of the bill for where a sports team worth $8.9 billion wants to play its overpriced games. There is no net benefit to the public, and we won't be taken again.</p><p><i>Kent Schielke, Wheaton</i></p><h3>Tan in, donkey out</h3><p>Forget the elephant. Forget the donkey.</p><p>At their next national convention, the Democrats should declare, “We are the party of the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/tansuit" target="_blank" >tan suit</a>.”</p><p><i>Mary and William Dodd Brown, Lincoln Square</i></p><h3>A lake take </h3><p>Donald Trump is not right about everything. In light of his countless extraordinary accomplishments and his indisputable personal magnificence, his renaming of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/27/trump-signs-order-renaming-lake-ontario-as-lake-america-in-the-united-states" >Lake Ontario to “Lake America” </a>is far too modest. Wouldn't it be so much more appropriate to rename it "Lake Trump?"</p><p>But, on second thought, he probably believes that Lake Superior has been named after him already.</p><p><i>Chet Alexander, Alsip</i></p><h3>Testing the waters </h3><p>Donald Trump renamed the wrong lake.</p><p>He should have renamed Lake Superior.</p><p>Are the other lakes "inferior?" This is politically incorrect!</p><p>Henceforth, Lake Superior: should be known as "Lake Equal."</p><p><i>Robert E. Frey, West Ridge</i><br></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Boyfriend and his mom tell people that they are siblings
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My boyfriend, "Evan," and his mother, "Mitzi," tell people they are siblings. I love my boyfriend, but I don't feel comfortable lying for him, and I wish he wouldn't lie for his mother. Evan is in his early 30s. His mother is in her early 50s, though she tells people she is 10 years younger.</p><p>Mitzi has worked in the hospitality industry since Evan was a young child. Back then, she claims restaurant managers wouldn't give parents preferred shifts due to their childcare-related schedule conflicts. For her entire career, she has kept up the lie that she's younger than she is and childless, and that Evan is actually her brother. She now claims that if the managers she works for knew her real age, they would discriminate against her because she's older than the other young, hip bartenders.</p><p>Evan has worked with his mother at several restaurants and has helped her keep up the lie with co-workers and mutual friends they have met at various jobs over the years. My instincts tell me the real reason his mother doesn't fess up now is because she doesn't want to tell longtime acquaintances she has been lying to them for years.</p><p>I wouldn't want to blow her cover if this false narrative really protects her in her industry. There have been several instances where I have interacted with these misinformed friends, and it makes me extremely uncomfortable. Evan hasn't asked me to lie to his friends for him, but I know if I don't, his social circle would be confused and likely hurt. I don't want to lie, but I'm also scared of the consequences of telling the truth or accidentally spilling the beans. Please help! — <i>TANGLED WEB</i></p><p><b>DEAR TANGLED WEB:</b> Do any of these folks come out and ask you how old Evan's mother is or whether they might not be brother and sister? Ageism is a fact, and many people lie about their ages for any number of reasons. If being involved with two people who are untruthful about their circumstances makes you uncomfortable, then you need to rethink the relationship. From where I sit, you are about to put your foot on the third rail, my dear, and if you do, it doesn't take a crystal ball to predict that your relationship with your boyfriend and his mother will vaporize.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am a 28-year-old woman who can't stop overthinking. Lately, more than ever, I realize that I'm still alone, have not found anybody to settle down with and have no children. When I scroll on social media, I see all my friends who have recently married or had babies. It appears that they are all progressing and are happily content. Am I doing something wrong? Where should I be spending my time? Am I worried about the wrong things? Should I just let things be the way they are? — <i>OVERLOOKED IN IOWA</i></p><p><b>DEAR OVERLOOKED:</b> Please stop comparing yourself to your friends. What you perceive they have is not important. Think honestly about your own life and desires. Are you actually lonely? If so, seek out social groups in your areas of interest. As you make new friends, remember to stay open to romance, but don't obsess about it. If you simply try to have fun with people, you may be surprised by what develops.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Why did bridges in Chicago get stuck due to heat? Can it happen again?
entries.summary: <p>On Wednesday, two Chicago bridges <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/09/02/lake-shore-drive-bridge-river?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=090326%20Morning%20Edition&utm_content=090326%20Morning%20Edition+CID_e22e13e556e7c07976399b015e30215f&utm_source=cst_campaign_monitor&utm_term=Bridges%20stuck%20in%20heat&tpcc=cst_cm" target="_blank" ><u>got stuck</u></a> in a raised position due to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/09/01/september-october-chicago-heat-wave-is-this-normal" target="_blank" ><u>severe heat</u></a>. The stuck bridges caused hours of disruptions and traffic jams.</p><h3>What happened?</h3><p>The DuSable Lake Shore Drive bridge was closed for more than four hours. It got stuck after a routine lift around 10 a.m. to let a yacht pass.</p><p>Crews spent hours trying to close the bridge completely. A Chicago Fire Department boat sprayed water to cool it down on Wednesday, which was Chicago’s second day <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/09/01/september-october-chicago-heat-wave-is-this-normal" target="_blank" ><u>under a heat advisory</u></a>.</p><p>Then at 4:30 p.m., the Torrence Avenue Bridge — located over the Calumet River on the Far South Side — got stuck for more than an hour. “Thermal expansion caused by the high temperatures affected the bridge’s operation,” said a Chicago Department of Transportation spokesperson.</p><h3>Why did the bridges get stuck?</h3><p>“Extreme heat causes the metal on bridges to expand and cause jams which prohibit bridges from opening or closing,” the <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/CFDMedia/status/2095520139454132572" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Fire Department</u></a> said in an X post.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/09/03/extreme-heat-continues-in-chicago-area-thursday-ahead-of-cold-front-rain" target="_blank" ><u>Temperatures peaked</u></a> at 95 degrees Tuesday and 96 degrees Wednesday at O’Hare Airport, according to the National Weather Service. The heat index peaked at 106 degrees Tuesday at Midway Airport.</p><p>When closed, Chicago bascule bridges like DuSable Lake Shore Drive bridge are somewhat protected from thermal expansion due to cooler air from the river below, explained Jim Phillips, founder of website <a class="Link" href="https://chicagoloopbridges.com/" target="_blank" >ChicagoLoopBridges.com</a>. (Translated from French, "bascule" means "seesaw.")</p><p>“Once raised, the bridge leaf is exposed to higher temperatures and it expands,” he said. Sometimes the expansion “is enough to cause problems returning the leaf to the closed position.”</p><h3>Has this happened before?</h3><p>Yes. But it’s not very common.</p><p>ChicagoLoopBridges.com features a 2010 <a class="Link" href="https://chicagoloopbridges.com/FAQS12.html#ans1aaa" target="_blank" ><u>photo</u></a> showing workers hosing down the stuck and open State Street Bridge. That day, it was more than 85 degrees, according to the website.</p><p>Phillips lived in Chicago from 2008 to 2016 and followed most of the bridge lifts but never witnessed a thermal expansion problem himself. “As a Chicago bridge geek, I was disappointed,” he said.</p><h3>Could stuck bridges become more common in Chicago?</h3><p>As a city with so many older movable bridges and extreme hot and cold weather, Chicago is vulnerable to stuck bridges, said Joseph Schwieterman, director of DePaul University’s Sustainable Urban Development Program.</p><p>Chicago also has the most moveable bridges of any city in the U.S., making it potentially more vulnerable to heat-related closures, said Grace Truslow, policy analyst at the Eno Center for Transportation, a Washington D.C. think tank.</p><div Wednesday.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“Aging bridges often become misaligned due to wear and tear, minor bending and slight shifts in the pylons supporting them. That heightens the risk that they will not close properly,” added Schwieterman.</p><p>About 17% of Chicago’s bridges are “structurally deficient”, according to a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/04/27/bridge-condition-structurally-deficient" target="_blank" ><u>Sun-Times analysis</u></a>.</p><p>Exactly 100 of Chicago’s 601 bridges are listed in the same “poor” condition as the State Street Bridge, which unexpectedly shut down in April 2025.</p><p>That’s 16.6%, according the analysis of <a class="Link" href="https://geodata.bts.gov/datasets/usdot::national-bridge-inventory/explore?location=41.881786%2C-87.633027%2C11" target="_blank" ><u>federal bridge inspection records</u></a>, and well above the <a class="Link" href="https://infrastructurereportcard.org/cat-item/bridges-infrastructure/" target="_blank" ><u>national average of 6.7%</u></a>.</p><p>In March, the city <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/03/25/state-street-bridge-reopens" target="_blank" ><u>reopened the State Street Bridge</u></a> after nearly a year of emergency repairs.</p><h3>Do stuck bridges happen in other places? </h3><p>Yes. In 2024, New York’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=84lY2YiIhCI&t=1s" target="_blank" ><u>Third Avenue Bridge</u></a> on the Harlem River couldn’t close during extreme heat. Last year the <a class="Link" href="https://www.wmtw.com/article/casco-bay-bridge-stuck-open-traffic-south-portland-maine/65193904" target="_blank" ><u>Casco Bay Bridge</u></a> in South Portland, Maine, got stuck open.</p><p>“Movable bridges are at particular risk of operational delays due to heat because heat can disrupt the mechanical mechanisms that open and close bridges,” wrote Truslow in an <a class="Link" href="https://enotrans.org/article/extreme-heat-presents-risks-for-transportation-infrastructure/" target="_blank" ><u>Eno Center</u></a> article last week.</p><h3>Should Chicago not lift bridges in hot weather?</h3><p>That’s not realistic.</p><p>“So many vessels, including sailboats, use our river system that it is unrealistic to avoid opening and closing the bridges during heatwaves,” said Schwieterman.</p><p>“We can make modest adjustments, such as avoiding lifting them in the hottest part of the day, but we must provide nearly constant river access. The Chicago River is a federally designated navigable waterway, which limits our options,” he said.</p><p>The city <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/depts/cdot/provdrs/bridge/news/2026/april/cdot-announces-spring-bridge-lifts-along-the-chicago-river-start.html" target="_blank" ><u>schedules bridge lifts</u></a> in the spring and fall to let boat owners take their vessels in and out of storage.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>The Torrence Avenue Bridge — located on the city’s Far South Side — got stuck in the raised position on Wednesday, just hours after the DuSable Lake Shore Drive bridge reopened following a similar occurrence. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Spraying water on bridges can cool them. Officials can also monitor bridges with sensors and inspections “when temperatures rise above a certain threshold and preemptively decide to keep bridges opened or closed,” Truslow said.</p><h3>Has hotter weather affected other infrastructure?</h3><p>Definitely.</p><p>This summer, severe heat caused tire blowouts on <a class="Link" href="https://www.ksla.com/2026/07/22/road-buckling-tire-blowouts-reported-extreme-heat-grips-shreveport/" target="_blank" ><u>Interstate 49</u></a> in Louisiana and <a class="Link" href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/weather-news/articles/extreme-heat-put-greenville-roads-035900078.html" target="_blank" ><u>buckling pavement</u></a> on U.S. Highway 69 in Greenville, Texas, according to Eno Center.</p><p>Extreme and frequent temperature increases have caused concrete to expand and roads to buckle. <a class="Link" href="https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/how-extreme-heat-harms-planes-trains-water-mains-and-other-crucial/" target="_blank" ><u>Asphalt softens</u></a> in heat and can warp.</p><p>Extreme heat can cause rail, bridge and overhead wires to expand. Amtrak may enact heat restrictions that require trains to reduce speed, which can result in possible delays.</p><p>Transportation infrastructure is not designed for extreme levels of heat these days, wrote Truslow for Eno Center. “Transportation agencies, airport operators, and rail operators must be planning for a present and future with higher average temperatures.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/04/27/bridge-condition-structurally-deficient" >1 in 6 Chicago bridges are in ‘poor’ condition. How worried should you be?</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/09/02/lake-shore-drive-bridge-river" >Another Chicago bridge gets stuck in sweltering heat hours after DuSable Lake Shore Drive bridge reopens</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Nearly a year after the South Shore raid forced him from his home, one former resident is still homeless
entries.summary: <p>On a tree-lined street on Chicago’s South Side, Darren Hightower rearranges some items in the backseat of his decades-old Chevy Trailblazer. This SUV is where he’s been sleeping most nights recently.</p><p>“I just lay my seat back in here, crack my windows [open],” he says. “I probably got some clothes back there, but I don't make it look like I live in there.”</p><p>Hightower is one of dozens of former residents of 7500 S. South Shore Dr., a troubled apartment complex in Chicago’s South Shore neighborhood that was raided last September by federal agents during Operation Midway Blitz, the Trump administration’s sweeping enforcement campaign.</p><p>Not long after the raid, a Cook County judge ordered Hightower and dozens of other residents to vacate the building, calling it a "fire trap." Judge Debra Seaton said she was protecting residents from danger.</p><p>“This court is not making anybody homeless," she said.</p><p>Hightower, 41, begs to differ. Now, nearly a year after the raid, he and many of his neighbors are still stuck in limbo, unable to secure housing and unsure of where to go.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/immigration/2025/10/01/massive-immigration-raid-on-chicago-apartment-building-leaves-residents-reeling-i-feel-defeated?subscription=true" target="_blank" ><u>raid</u></a> was one of the definitive moments of Operation Midway Blitz. After midnight on Sept. 30, federal agents rappelled down from helicopters, ransacked the building, and zip-tied residents, including many U.S. citizens. The government said it was going after members of the Venezuelan gang Tren de Aragua, but no criminal charges have been filed against anyone who was arrested that night.</p><p>The raid set off a chain of events that laid bare the precariousness of Chicago’s housing system for the city’s low-income renters: the lack of affordable apartments for both <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/immigration/2026/04/08/chicagos-migrants-face-scams-sky-high-rents-and-squalor-in-search-for-housing?subscription=true" target="_blank" ><u>migrants</u></a> and U.S. citizens, the disinvestment from <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/housing/2025/11/25/sausage-king-of-chicago-south-side-housing-slum-section-8-alan-smolinisky-brian-chen?subscription=true" target="_blank" ><u>out-of-town landlords</u></a>, the neglect from property managers, a broken and inefficient courts system, and a virtually nonexistent safety net for the working homeless.</p><p>Hightower has experienced all of the above.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>In this photo from December 2025, Darren Hightower searches apartment listings hoping to find a new place to live. Hightower had to leave his home in South Shore after a judge ordered residents to vacate the apartment complex.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Esther Yoon-Ji Kang |WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>The search for a home</h3><p>On a freezing day a couple of weeks before Christmas last year, he put most of his belongings in storage and <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/housing/2025/12/12/move-out-date-arrives-chicago-building-raided-feds-one-resident-looks-back-ahead?subscription=true" target="_blank" ><u>moved out</u></a>. He and <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/housing/2025/12/12/last-remaining-residents-move-out-troubled-south-shore-building-raided-feds?subscription=true" target="_blank" ><u>dozens of others</u></a> scattered throughout the city, many of them finding shelter in hotels paid for by Catholic Charities.</p><p>The funds only covered two weeks, so after he left the hotel, Hightower headed to a friend’s place. He stayed there for a few months but wore out his welcome, and has been crashing on couches or sleeping in his truck for the past few months.</p><p>The housing search has been brutal, Hightower says. His work schedule makes it hard to go to apartment showings, the application fees are high, and landlords don’t call back. But the biggest problem is the sky-high rents — especially for the “slum-like” apartments he’s seen.</p><p>“You go to some of these places, you can see five guys sitting out here selling, you can see the infestation from pests and rodents,” he says. “Some people may call me picky, but I'm not gonna go somewhere I'm still gonna be uncomfortable and be paying a bunch of money. That doesn't fit well with me at all.”</p><p>Hightower adds that landlords are charging $1,000 to $1,200 dollars for a studio, which is well over his budget, after a wrist injury at his warehouse job resulted in reduced hours. He feels demoralized to have a job and still not be able to afford a clean and safe home.</p><p>“When you have somebody who's actually working, and they're still out on the streets, still don't have any foundation for themselves, it sucks,” he says.</p><p>Years ago, he was approved for a subsidized apartment through the Chicago Housing Authority. But he still sits on a wait list. When Hightower logs into the CHA portal, it shows an estimated wait time of “more than 25 years.”</p><p>“It is what it is,” Hightower says. “They may call me sooner, they may never call me. I can't wait on that. I just have to keep trying to figure it out for myself.”</p><p>When asked if he would consider going to one of the city’s homeless shelters, he shakes his head. Hightower has been in homeless shelters before, as a kid, and doesn’t want to go back.</p><p>“A shelter is like prison in its own way,” he says. “[There are] rules and regulations you have to abide by. You might have a time that you have to be there in the evening, you can't be there during the day, you have to protect your possessions. It’s not something I would wanna go through again.”</p><p>So for now, he chooses his car.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Resident Darren Hightower speaks during a press conference at the 7500 South Shore apartment complex on the South Side, Monday, Dec. 8, 2025. The complex was raided by federal agents on September 30th during Operation Midway Blitz and now tenants are being forced to vacate by the end of the week. | Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>The cost of homelessness</h3><p>Jonah Karsh, a housing organizer with the Metropolitan Tenants Organization (MTO), says Hightower is not the only resident from the South Shore building still struggling to secure housing.</p><p>As of March, Karsh says, at least 17 families from the South Shore building were still without permanent housing, staying with relatives and friends or living in their vehicles. A handful of people had found new places to live, especially if they had housing vouchers through CHA. Dozens more were unreachable, with many phone numbers disconnected.</p><p>“The overwhelming feeling was dejection and resignation,” he said of his conversations with former tenants of the building.</p><p>Karsh says the immigration raid was an “extraordinary” event, but what happened in the building before and after was “not unusual at all." The conditions there and the aftermath reflect the intractable and systemic housing problems in Chicago, he says, and usually, “the tenants are the ones who pay the price.”</p><p>Darren Hightower says what happened to the tenants from 7500 S. South Shore Dr. could have been prevented.</p><p>“[There’s] a ton of things that could have been done to avoid people thrown out on the street or forced out of their homes,” he says.</p><p>Hightower believes the Wisconsin-based landlord, Trinity Flood, could have invested in the building instead of milking it for profit. The old property managers could have repaired broken elevators and provided security. The judge could have ordered the court-appointed receiver who replaced the property manager to fix the hazardous conditions. She could have given residents more time to find new homes.</p><p>But none of that happened, Hightower says, and now he and others bear the cost of homelessness.</p><p>Not having an apartment has taken a toll on his sleep, his eating, and even his work, he says.</p><p>But the hardest part is how helpless he feels. Hightower takes pride in doing things for others and doesn’t want his loved ones to know what he’s going through. He says without the foundation of a home, he “can’t do anything for anybody” — not for his siblings, his nieces and nephew, or for his friends.</p><p>Despite feeling this way sometimes, Hightower tries to look on the bright side.</p><p>“I still have my job, I still have my vehicle, I still have my health, I still have my looks — look at me,” he says, laughing.</p><p>He’s not sure where he’ll be when the cold weather sets in, especially since his car has been giving him trouble lately. But he hopes he will find an affordable apartment before it gets too chilly.</p><p>For now, he says, “I’m a rolling stone — doing what I gotta do and staying where I can just to get by.”</p>

entries.title: 10 storefront theater shows to see in Chicago this fall
entries.summary: <p>Fall always brings a focus on the big regional theaters, and this season delivers. <a class="Link" href="https://lookingglasstheatre.org/" target="_blank" ><u>Lookingglass </u></a>is staging Gregg Ostrin’s “Kowalski,” starring Emmy nominee Johnny Galecki (“Roseanne,” “Big Bang Theory”).<a class="Link" href="https://www.steppenwolf.org/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24148500398&gbraid=0AAAAADOpBXQ_KlPgcZ5wiTEXdg1exPt4_&gclid=Cj0KCQjwteTUBhD4ARIsAEYjs3pSGkQns2A7bLdeJQjxuFW6xbvT1RNVZi2hpbGuuS8jtUBtUzPHgewaAqPIEALw_wcB" target="_blank" ><u> Steppenwolf’s</u></a> scathing drama “Topdog/Underdog,” which won writer Suzan–Lori Parks a Pulitzer, puts Tony nominee Glenn Davis toe-to-toe with Namir Smallwood, who was recently on Broadway in Tracy Letts’ drama “Bug.”</p><p>But as the Broadway in Chicago remount of Kokandy’s hit musical <a class="Link" href="https://www.broadwayinchicago.com/shows/jekyll-hyde/" target="_blank" ><u>“Jekyll & Hyde”</u></a> illustrates (opening Sept. 8), the place to see the next big thing is on the city’s storefront stages. So I decided to focus my fall 2026 list in Off Loop, neighborhood theaters.</p><p>Here are 10 shows to see this season on Chicago’s smaller and midsize stages.</p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.prometheantheatre.org/project/blood-of-the-lamb/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Blood of the Lamb </u></b></a><b>(Chicago premiere)</b></h3><p><b>Where: </b>The Den Theatre, presented by<b> </b>Promethean Theatre Ensemble<br><b>When:</b> Through Oct. 3</p><p>What storefront theater lacks in budget, it recoups through creativity. This two-hander, by playwright Arlene Hutton ( “Last Train to Nibroc”), is a thriller set two days from right now. A woman on a cross-country flight from California to New York is diverted and detained in Dallas. She wants on the next flight out, but being pregnant, in Texas, turns that into a political problem. The production, helmed by Chicago director Anna C. Bahow, splits the two roles between four actors in a cast that includes two-time Jeff nominee Meghann Tabor and Promethean ensemble member Heather Dennis. <i>1331 N. Milwaukee Ave.</i></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.definitiontheatre.org/shows/hwgo" target="_blank" ><b><u>How We Got On</u></b></a> <b>(world premiere)</b></h3><p><b>Where:</b> Definition Theatre<br><b>When</b>: Sept. 11–27</p><p>Hyde Park’s Definition Theatre deserves attention. Operating across the street from the University of Chicago’s Court Theatre, Definition is known for staging new works by emerging playwrights, with ensemble member James Ijames winning the Pulitzer for his play “Fat Ham.” The world premiere “How We Got on,” directed by founding Artistic Director Tyrone Phillips, is written by theater vet Idris Goodwin, who uses music in the storytelling. This world premiere follows three suburban teens who discover hip-hop and have their lives forever changed. <i>1160 E. 55th St.</i></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div ><b><u>Bonnie’s Last Flight</u></b></a><b> (world premiere)</b></h3><p><b>Where:</b> Rivendell Theatre<br><b>When:</b> Sept. 12–Oct. 17</p><p>Written by Eliza Bent, this production is technically a quirky workplace comedy, which we’re all pretty familiar with. Here’s the rub: this workplace is an airplane. Jan, played by Jeff Award winner Rebecca Spence (“Every Brilliant Thing”), is taking her last flight and everyone knows except her best friend, Greig, played by Paul Oakley Stovall (Tony Award for producing “A Strange Loop”). Director Devon de Mayo will have her hands full creating action in the contained tubular body of a plane. But she has excellent actors to work with as the cast also includes Jeff Award winner Jessica Ervin (Rivendell’s “Motherhouse”), LaKecia Harris (Manual Cinema's “A Christmas Carol”) and Glenn Obrero, who had memorable roles in Rivendell’s “Pivot” and A Red Orchid’s “The Targeted.” <i>5779 N. This show will be Raven’s first time staging a full-on musical (and WBEZ will be there to host <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-club" target="_blank" ><u>Theater Club</u></a> on Oct. 18). Directed by the Chicago based multi-Jeff Award-winner Mikael Burke (Remy Bumpo’s “Blues for an Alabama Sky” and Refracted Theatre’s “Tambo & Bones"), this Chicago premiere is one of the most anticipated shows on this list. The production, written by Michael R. Jackson, won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama in 2020 and the Tony for Best New Musical in 2022. The story follows Usher, a Black queer playwright (Eddie Weaver) working as an usher on Broadway. He’s struggling to write a play — about a Black queer usher on Broadway who is struggling to write a play. It’s heady, time-loopy and set to music. <i>6157 N. Clark St.</i></p><h3></h3><h3><a class="Link" href="https://thefactorytheater.com/portfolio/radical-futures/" target="_blank" ><b><u>Radical Futures</u></b></a><b> (world premiere)</b></h3><p><b>Where:</b> The Factory Theater<br><b>When: </b>Oct. 16–Nov. 21</p><p>Shows like this are what make Chicago storefront special. (I recently visited the Factory Theater for Strawdog’s “Advance Man” and it was <i>so weird</i>… I loved it.) These companies take swings and stage shows that may be weird, or wonky or in this case, a risky new sci-fi production, that may or may not work — but will definitely be fun. “Radical Futures,” written by B.Z. Florida, who writes sci-fi plays and comics, is set in a place Chicagoans have a soft spot for: a dive bar. That’s a good start. From that familiar place things take a strange turn. Directed by Kayla Menz, this production asks: Can we change our futures? Are the friends we currently hold close going to be there in the long run? Does it matter? The journey sounds interesting. <i>1623 W. Howard St. </i></p><h3><a class="Link" href="https://www.eventbrite.com/e/a-clockwork-orange-tickets-1982193806033" target="_blank" ><b><u>A Clockwork Orange: A Play with Music</u></b></a><b> </b></h3><p><b>Where:</b> The Chopin Theatre, presented by Kokandy Productions<br><b>When: </b>Nov. 5–Jan. 10</p><p>Kokandy has a reputation for taking big Broadway musicals and cleverly staging them in a Wicker Park basement theater. This musical version of Stanley Kubrick’s cult classic film was adapted by Anthony Burgess, who wrote the original novel. Burgess crafted the play with the intention of it being staged with limited sets and props. Kokandy hasn’t announced casting, but artistic director Derek Van Barham will direct and Breon Arzell will choreograph, which is a promising place to start. The material itself is rather graphic, and the idea of setting it to Beethoven-inspired music is… an intriguing cap for the fall season. <i>1543 W. Division St.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-a60000" name="module-a60000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>For more theater coverage:</h3><ul id="rte-62d951e2-a7d8-11f1-bb92-332fce658ca0"><li>It took a decade, and $32 million, to make the idea of <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2026/09/03/evanston-northlight-theater-chicago-suburbs-arts-annex" target="_blank" ><u>Evanston’s Northlight Theater </u></a>a reality</li><li>Ahead of a new show at Victory Gardens, playwright and author <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2026/09/01/heir-to-a-revolutionary-past-playwright-and-author-zayd-ayers-dohrn-charts-his-own-path" target="_blank" ><u>Zayd Ayers Dohrn</u></a> charts his own path</li><li><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/theater-stages/2026/08/20/theater-club-timeline-raven-northlight-tickets" target="_blank" ><u>WBEZ’s Theater Club</u></a> makes a return for the fall theater season</li></ul></div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: No relief from the heat as September kicks off. Is this normal?
entries.summary: <p>Sept. 1 was the start of meteorological fall — but also the start of yet another heat wave in the Chicago area. A heat advisory was issued by Chicago's Office of Emergency Management and Communications for "dangerous heat" on Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday and Friday.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/31/temperature-heat-forecast" target="_blank" ><u>Peak heat indices</u></a> — reflecting how the temperature feels — are expected to reach 104 degrees Friday due to humidity before <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/09/04/heat-advisory" target="_blank" >the warning </a>expires at 10 p.m., according to the National Weather Service. Temperatures are expected to rise to 95 degrees in northern Illinois and northwest Indiana. </p><h3>Is it unusual for September to be so hot?</h3><p>This week’s high temperatures, the result of a heat dome moving into the area, will keep temperatures about 10 degrees above the normal average for late August and early September, said Zachary Yack, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Romeoville.</p><p>This heat wave is “somewhat unusual and a significant and potentially dangerous late-season event,” said Ashish Sharma, climate and urban sustainability lead at Discovery Partners Institute at University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. “Chicago’s normal high in this period is about 80 degrees.”</p><p>But hot Septembers are not new. In 2015, the National Weather Service answered the question “<a class="Link" href="https://www.weather.gov/ilx/sep2015-heat" target="_blank" ><u>How unusual is this September heat wave?</u></a>”</p><p>The answer: not that unusual.</p><p>“Looking back at the climate statistics since 1980, there have generally been about 3 days per September with highs of at least 90 degrees. This does not happen every year, but is somewhat regular,” the NWS wrote in 2015.</p><h3>Does it feel hotter because it’s been such a hot summer?</h3><p>Maybe. In July, Chicago had two heat waves in which the temperatures topped 90 degrees.</p><p>“There is probably some heat fatigue for Chicagoans," Sharma said. "Many of us are mentally and physically tired of it.</p><p>“Chicago’s July was warmer than normal. This late burst of heat adds to an already demanding summer, especially when people were looking for more pleasant weather in September after schools are reopened."</p><p>The heat has taken a toll. In August, Cook County recorded its 13th <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/20/cook-county-records-13th-heat-death-of-2026-more-than-doubling-previous-decade-high" target="_blank" ><u>heat death</u></a> of the year.</p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/30/extreme-heat-wave-death-chicago-cook-county-oak-lawn-july-stroke-stress-elderly-air-conditioning" target="_blank" ><u>WBEZ and Chicago Sun-Times analysis</u></a> of medical examiner data showed that Cook County has had more deaths related to the heat in 2026 than any other year in the last decade. Heat deaths previously peaked in Cook County in 2019 and 2022, with six deaths each of those years.</p><h3>Does it feel hotter because it’s humid?</h3><p>Yes. And maybe because of corn.</p><p>“When the air contains a great deal of moisture, sweat cannot evaporate as efficiently, and evaporation is the body’s primary cooling mechanism," Sharma said. "That is why an air temperature in the mid-90s can produce a heat index near 105 degrees and locally close to 110.</p><p>“The National Weather Service also points to moisture moving into the region and evapotranspiration from crops, sometimes called ‘corn sweat,’ as contributors to the high humidity."</p><h3>Does it feel hotter because the weather has been more extreme?</h3><p>Maybe. This summer, the Chicago area has been pummeled by heat waves, tornadoes, storms, flooding and wildfire smoke.</p><p>As of the end of August, 207 <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/08/27/200-tornadoes-illinois-2026" target="_blank" ><u>tornadoes</u></a> have touched down in Illinois this year. The previous record of 142 was set just two years ago, according to Trent Ford, the Illinois state climatologist. This is the third year in a row that Illinois has experienced a triple-digit tornado season. The state’s average is closer to <a class="Link" href="https://stateclimatologist.isws.illinois.edu/climate-of-illinois/tornadoes-in-illinois/" target="_blank" ><u>50</u></a>.</p><p>The Chicago area also has seen some of the most severe storms in recent years this summer, and they have caused damage to homes, widespread flooding, and for the first time, nearly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/07/06/chicago-deep-tunnel-historic-flooding-tarp-reservoir-weather-climate-change" target="_blank" ><u>filled the reservoirs</u></a> meant to manage stormwater and flooding.</p><p></p><p>If anyone is craving fall sweater weather, they will have to grab some sunscreen instead.</p>

entries.title: Woman gunned down while walking in Englewood
entries.summary: <p>Police are looking for the assailant who opened fire at a 37-year-old woman, killing her Friday morning in Englewood. </p><p>It happened about 7:30 a.m. in the 6700 block of South Peoria Avenue, according to police, who said that she was walking outside when someone shot her once to the chest and back. </p><p>The unidentified woman was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center, where she was pronounced dead, according to police.</p><p>Area 1 detectives are investigating.<br></p>

entries.title: Chicago under heat warning for 4th day
entries.summary: <p>High temperatures and humidity could make it feel like 104 degrees in the Chicago area on Friday, as dangerous heat hits the area for the fourth day in a row.</p><p>The National Weather Service issued a heat advisory until 10 p.m. Friday for northern Illinois and northwest Indiana.</p><p>Temperatures are expected to rise to 95 degrees in the afternoon, according to the weather service. The humidity will make it feel more like 104 degrees.</p><p>Due to the heat, Chicago Public Schools said it would cancel outdoor activities or, if possible, hold them inside to "ensure students and staff are healthy, safe, and comfortable" for at least the second day in a row.</p><p>A chance of evening thunderstorms will be followed by an expected overnight low of 74 degrees, according to the forecast.</p><p>Chicago has been under a heat-related advisory every day since Tuesday, when the temperature at O'Hare Airport peaked at 95 degrees. Wednesday's recorded high was 96 degrees. Thursday's was 91 degrees.</p><p>The heat is forecast to be more extreme farther south of Chicago on Friday, as it has been for the entire week. The heat index on Friday could rise to the 105-110 degree range in Will County and parts of DuPage County, according to the weather service.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div
