entries.title: Chicago Packer: Jayden Reed wears West Side childhood on his arm
entries.summary: <p>GREEN BAY, Wis. — As a kid, Jayden Reed was a Bears fan. Growing up on the West Side of Chicago, his favorite player was Devin Hester. He watched in dismay as the Packers beat the Bears in the NFC Championship Game after the 2010 regular season.</p><p>As an adult, he plays wide receiver for the Packers. He has tried coaxing friends into switching sides in the NFL’s longest rivalry. And he just loves living in Green Bay.</p><p>“Everybody’s super nice out here,” he told the Sun-Times last week. “I love it just because it’s so low-key. It’s chill. Family and football — that’s all that it’s about here. Easy to save money.”</p><p>Not that he needs to. In April, the 26-year-old signed a three-year, $50.25 million contract extension that includes $20 million guaranteed. He’s well worth it. Among wide receivers with at least 100 targets since 2023, Reed is first in the NFL in passer rating when targeted (126.6).</p><p>But he’s a Chicago kid behind enemy lines, and he wears his hometown on his sleeve — or right beneath it. Tattooed on his upper left arm are street signs of the intersection where he grew up — Lamon and Cortez —with five cousins sleeping in one bedroom.</p><p>Reed said football was his only outlet. In eighth grade, he moved to Crest Hill. He moved to Aurora before his freshman year at Metea Valley. Before his senior year, he transferred to Naperville Central, where he earned All-Area honors from the Sun-Times.</p><p>After one year at Western Michigan, Reed transferred to Michigan State, where he earned second-team All-Big Ten honors as a senior and went to the Packers in the second round (50th overall) of the 2023 draft.</p><p>Reed said it’s still odd when he plays with the Packers at Soldier Field, where he went as a kid.</p><p>“That’s probably the most money I spend on games,” Reed said of securing tickets for friends and family. “It’s surreal just being able to go back and play at home. I get a little smack talk from some friends; some support from some friends. Kind of switched some of my friends over.”</p><p>He said he never envisioned himself with the Packers as he pursued his NFL dream, but he certainly wasn’t picky on draft day. Allegiances tend to change depending on who signs the paychecks, and the Packers made quite a commitment to Reed this year.</p><p>They made an even bigger one to top receiver Christian Watson, giving him a four-year, $92 million extension with $31 million guaranteed. And with more expected from 2025 first-round pick Matthew Golden (23rd overall), the Packers have a trio that will spell trouble for the Bears.</p><p>Reed led the Packers in receptions and receiving yards in his first two seasons, but he was limited to seven games last season because of a broken clavicle he suffered in Week 2 while stretching for what would’ve been a 39-yard touchdown had it not been negated by a penalty.</p><p>He looked like his usual self in training camp, almost a year removed from surgery. The Packers’ offense looked pretty good, too.</p><p>“We’ve been balling out all camp,” Reed said.</p><p>He has been a perfect role model for Golden, who appreciates the type of player Reed is.</p><p>“He can play anywhere; he can play inside, outside,” Golden said. “Just watching him since I first got here, the way he attacks practice and how he carries himself, it translates to the game. You can see the confidence that he has. I’m glad I get to play alongside him.</p><p>“He’s a YAC [yards after catch] monster. As long as he can get the ball in his hands, he’s real special after that, being able to make guys miss and get upfield.”</p><p>Reed will return to Chicago with the Packers for a Christmas Day game that could be a big one. If he thinks he has spent a lot of money on family and friends before, wait until he sees that bill.</p>

href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydana-l-i/" target="_blank" >Nearly a year after the South Shore raid forced him from his home, he’s still homeless</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydana-l-d/" target="_blank" >Esther Yoon-Ji Kang</a></h5><p><b>Blitz backstory</b>: On Sept. 30, 2025, federal agents raided a troubled South Shore apartment building — rappelling down from helicopters, ransacking the building and zip-tying residents, including many U.S. citizens, in one of the defining moments of the Trump administration's anti-immigration campaign, Operation Midway Blitz. The feds said they were going after Venezuelan gang members, but no criminal charges have been filed against anyone detained that night. A county judge soon ordered residents to vacate the building.</p><p><b>Key context</b>: The raid set off a chain of events that laid bare the precariousness of Chicago's housing system for the city’s low-income renters: the lack of affordable apartments for both migrants and U.S. citizens, the disinvestment from out-of-town landlords, the neglect from property managers, a broken and inefficient courts system, and a virtually nonexistent safety net for the working homeless.</p><p><b>After the operation</b>: Nearly a year after the raid, Darren Hightower, 41, is one of several former residents of the building stuck in limbo, unable to secure housing and unsure of where to go. Yee</a></h5><p><b>Broken bridges</b>: On Wednesday, two Chicago bridges got stuck in a raised position due to severe heat: the DuSable Lake Shore Drive bridge, closed for more than four hours, and the Torrence Avenue Bridge, closed for more than an hour. The stuck bridges caused hours of disruption and traffic jams.</p><p><b>Blame the heat</b>: The bridges, when closed, can be protected from thermal expansion, thanks to the cooler temperatures of the lake and river — raising them exposes the metal to the elements and allows the metal to expand, preventing the bridges from being closed, one expert said.</p><p><b>Will this happen again?</b> Chicago, with more movable bridges than any other U.S. city, is vulnerable to stuck bridges thanks to extreme hot and cold weather, experts said. Many of Chicago's bridges are aging, with about 17% considered "structurally deficient," a <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydana-l-q/" target="_blank" >Sun-Times >Mural is an ode to a couple of cowgirls</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydana-l-tr/" target="_blank" >Genevieve Bookwalter</a></h5><p>When Ruby Bean heard the call for an Andersonville mural inspired by lesbianism, she knew the cowgirls would be perfect.</p><p>"Chicago has a rich history with cowgirls, and same with Texas," said Bean, a Texas native. "A lot of my art has to do with capturing their histories."</p><p>So Bean submitted her design: two cowgirls "who are in love and holding hands." The colors of the desert at sunset behind them are also the colors from the lesbian flag, dark orange graduating down to dark pink. The white of the fence the two cowgirls lean against represents the equality sign.</p><p>The idea was perfect for Searah Deysach, owner of the feminist sex toy shop Early to Bed and the building that houses it at 5138 N. Clark St.</p><p>"I thought we had an opportunity to take advantage of putting more art and more queer art into the neighborhood," Deysach said.</p><p>The idea of cowgirls tracks for Andersonville. It's adjacent to the Uptown neighborhood that was <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydana-l-ty/" target="_blank" >once a draw for those moving from Appalachia and other spots in rural America, bringing their country music with them</a>.</p><p>As for the mural, Bean said, "I think that the important parts are it's just a celebration of love and stories that are untold."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydana-l-tj/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p><b>Say you've been tasked with compiling a playlist for future generations to capture the sound and essence of music from Chicago — what song absolutely needs to be included? Tell us why. 🎶</b></p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply to this question via email</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). We may run your answer in a future newsletter or story.</i></p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times Morning Edition!<br>Got a story you think we missed? <a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >Email us here.</a></p><hr><p><b>Written and curated by</b>: Matt Moore<br><b>Editor</b>: Satchel Price</p>

entries.title: Así afecta el calor extremo a los puentes móviles de Chicago. ¿Podrían los puentes atascados convertirse en algo normal en el futuro?
entries.summary: <p>El miércoles, dos puentes de Chicago <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/09/02/lake-shore-drive-bridge-river?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=090326%20Morning%20Edition&utm_content=090326%20Morning%20Edition+CID_e22e13e556e7c07976399b015e30215f&utm_source=cst_campaign_monitor&utm_term=Bridges%20stuck%20in%20heat&tpcc=cst_cm" target="_blank" >quedaron atascados</a> en posición elevada debido al calor extremo. Cuando los puentes se atascan provocaron horas de interrupciones y embotellamientos.</p><p>El Puente DuSable Lake Shore Drive quedó atascado por más de cuatro horas tras una elevación de rutina alrededor de las 10 a.m. el miércoles para dejar pasar un yate.</p><p>Los equipos pasaron horas intentando bajar completamente el puente. Un bote del Departamento de Bomberos de Chicago roció agua para enfriarlo, que fue el segundo día de la ciudad bajo un aviso de calor.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-290000" name="module-290000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Luego, a las 4:30 p.m., el Puente de Torrence Avenue —situado sobre el Río Calumet en el extremo sur de la ciudad— quedó atascado por más de una hora.</p><p>"La expansión térmica causada por las altas temperaturas afectó la operación del puente", dijo un portavoz del Departamento de Transporte de Chicago.</p><h3>¿Por qué se atascan los puentes?</h3><p>"El calor extremo hace que el metal de los puentes se expanda y provoque atascos que impiden que los puentes se abran o cierren", dijo el <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/CFDMedia/status/2095520139454132572" target="_blank" >Departamento de Bomberos de Chicago</a> en una publicación en X.</p><p>Las temperaturas alcanzaron los 95 grados Fahrenheit el martes y 96 grados el miércoles en el Aeropuerto O’Hare, según el Servicio Meteorológico Nacional. El índice de calor alcanzó 106 grados el martes en el Aeropuerto Midway.</p><p>Cuando están cerrados, los puentes basculantes de Chicago como el puente DuSable Lake Shore Drive están algo protegidos de la expansión térmica por el aire más frío del río debajo, explicó Jim Phillips, fundador del sitio web ChicagoLoopBridges.com.</p><p>"Una vez levantada, la plataforma del puente queda expuesta a temperaturas más altas y se expande", dijo. A veces la expansión "es suficiente para causar problemas al devolver la plataforma a la posición cerrada".</p><h3>¿Ha sucedido esto antes?</h3><p>Sí. Pero no es muy común.</p><p>ChicagoLoopBridges.com muestra una <a class="Link" href="https://chicagoloopbridges.com/FAQS12.html#ans1aaa" target="_blank" >foto</a> de 2010 en la que trabajadores están regando el Puente State Street, que quedó abierto y atascado ese día. Según el sitio, la temperatura superaba los 85 grados.</p><p>Phillips vivió en Chicago de 2008 a 2016 y siguió la mayoría de las elevaciones de puentes, pero nunca fue testigo de un problema por expansión térmica. "Como aficionado a los puentes de Chicago, me decepcionó", comentó.</p><h3>¿Podrían volverse más comunes los puentes atascados en Chicago?</h3><p>Como ciudad con tantos puentes móviles antiguos y con temperaturas extremas, Chicago es vulnerable a tener puentes atascados, dijo Joseph Schwieterman, director del Programa de Desarrollo Urbano Sostenible de la Universidad DePaul.</p><p>Chicago también tiene más puentes movibles que cualquier otra ciudad en Estados Unidos, lo que la hace potencialmente más vulnerable a cierres por calor, dijo Grace Truslow, analista de políticas del Eno Center for Transportation, un centro de estudios de Washington D.C.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" para enfriarlo el miércoles.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>"Los puentes envejecidos a menudo quedan desalineados debido al desgaste, pequeñas deformaciones y ligeros desplazamientos en los pilares que los sostienen. Eso aumenta el riesgo de que no cierren correctamente", añadió Schwieterman.</p><p>Un 17% de los puentes de Chicago están "estructuralmente deficientes", según un <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/04/27/bridge-condition-structurally-deficient" target="_blank" >análisis del Sun-Times</a>.</p><p>Exactamente 100 de los 601 puentes de Chicago figuran en la misma condición "pobre" que el Puente State Street, que se cerró inesperadamente en abril de 2025.</p><p>Eso es un 16.6%, según el análisis de los registros federales de inspección de puentes, y muy por encima del promedio nacional del 6.7%.</p><p>En marzo, la ciudad <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/03/25/state-street-bridge-reopens" target="_blank" >reabrió el Puente State Street</a> tras casi un año de reparaciones de emergencia.</p><h3>¿Hay puentes atascados en otros lugares?</h3><p>Sí. En 2024, el Puente Third Avenue de Nueva York sobre el Río Harlem no pudo cerrarse durante una ola de calor extrema. El año pasado el Puente Casco Bay en South Portland, Maine, quedó atascado en posición abierta.</p><p>"Los puentes movibles están particularmente en riesgo de retrasos operativos por el calor porque el calor puede afectar los mecanismos mecánicos que abren y cierran los puentes", escribió Truslow en un artículo del Eno Center la semana pasada.</p><h3>¿Debería Chicago dejar de elevar los puentes cuando hace calor?</h3><p>Eso no es realista.</p><p>"Tantas embarcaciones, incluyendo barcos de vela, usan nuestro sistema fluvial, lo que lo hace poco realista evitar abrir y cerrar los puentes durante las olas de calor", dijo Schwieterman.</p><p>"Podemos hacer ajustes modestos, como evitar levantarlos en la parte más calurosa del día, pero debemos mantener un acceso fluvial casi constante. El Río Chicago es una vía navegable designada por el gobierno federal, lo que limita nuestras opciones", dijo.</p><p>La Ciudad programa elevaciones de puentes en primavera y otoño para permitir que los propietarios de embarcaciones saquen y guarden sus naves.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>El puente Torrence Avenue —ubicado en el extremo sur de la ciudad— se quedó atascado en posición elevada el miércoles, apenas horas después de que el Puente DuSable Lake Shore Drive reabriera tras un incidente similar.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Rociar agua sobre los puentes puede enfriarlos. Las autoridades también pueden monitorear los puentes con sensores e inspecciones "cuando las temperaturas superan cierto umbral y decidir preventivamente mantener los puentes abiertos o cerrados", dijo Truslow.</p><h3>¿El clima más caluroso ha afectado otras infraestructuras?</h3><p>Definitivamente.</p><p>Este verano, el calor extremo provocó que llantas se reventaran en la Interestatal 49 en Luisiana y el levantamiento del pavimento en la carretera U.S. 69 en Greenville, Texas, según el Eno Center.</p><p>Los aumentos de temperatura extremos y frecuentes han hecho que el concreto se expanda y que las carreteras se deformen. El asfalto se ablanda con el calor y puede deformarse.</p><p>El calor extremo puede hacer que rieles, puentes y cables aéreos se expandan. Amtrak puede imponer restricciones por calor que obliguen a los trenes a reducir la velocidad, lo que puede generar retrasos.</p><p>La infraestructura de transporte no está diseñada para los niveles extremos de calor actuales, escribió Truslow para el Eno Center. "Las agencias de transporte, los operadores de aeropuertos y los operadores de ferrocarril deben planificar para un presente y un futuro con temperaturas promedio más altas".</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Once-secret records show grand jurors sought Bovino testimony, more evidence in doomed Midway Blitz cases
entries.summary: <p>Federal grand jurors listened<b> </b>to more than an hour<b> </b>of testimony<b> </b>last fall<b> </b>about a tussle between<b> </b>Operation Midway Blitz<b> </b>protester<b> </b>Cole<b> </b>Sheridan<b> </b>and<b> </b>then-U.S. Border Patrol Cmdr. Gregory Bovino — an event that lasted a matter of seconds.</p><p>Prosecutors said the Oct. 3 struggle<b> </b>left Bovino<b> </b>with a strained groin muscle. They said they had body-camera footage that captured part of the incident. And they delivered the testimony of at least two law enforcement officials<b> </b>while seeking an assault charge<b> </b>against Sheridan.</p><p>But it wasn’t enough. The grand jury wanted to hear from Bovino.</p><p>That rare insight from the grand jury room was revealed in court records unsealed this week at the request of the Chicago Sun-Times. They contain additional evidence that, far from being a rubber stamp for prosecutors, Chicago grand jurors repeatedly pushed for more information before handing up indictments during Midway Blitz, the deportation campaign marking its one-year anniversary Tuesday.</p><p>Prosecutors wound up <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/28/border-patrol-gregory-bovino-cole-sheridan-broadview-ice" target="_blank" >dropping Sheridan’s case</a> four days after<b> </b>the panel sought Bovino’s testimony. By then, video had surfaced<b> </b>that undermined the prosecution. And a judge <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/06/judge-sara-ellis-operation-midway-blitz-tear-gas-deportation-campaign" target="_blank" >accused Bovino of lying</a><b> </b>under oath<b> </b>that same week.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/bDO3pvTt4qY?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="The video that sank the federal case against Cole Sheridan"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Meanwhile, a grand jury considering a separate case<b> </b>asked for so much information<b> </b>that a prosecutor<b> </b>conceded<b> </b>the feds<b> </b>“cannot realistically obtain all of the evidence the grand jury has requested.”</p><p>Ultimately, it appears Chicago grand jurors joined their counterparts across the nation — most notably in Los Angeles and Washington — in forming a bulwark against the aggressive prosecutions that accompanied the Trump administration’s deportation efforts. Chicago panelists specifically refused to indict at least three<b> </b>of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/tracker-federal-prosecutions-chicago-status-trumps-immigration-blitz-ice" target="_blank" >33<b> </b>known Midway Blitz defendants</a>.</p><p>One grand juror famously called the tainted “Broadview Six” case <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/06/09/broadview-six-grand-jury-midway-blitz-boutros-trump?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=061026%20Morning%20Edition&utm_content=061026%20Morning%20Edition+CID_e5cb798cbab6da1240e3e04b560963b8&utm_source=cst_campaign_monitor&utm_term=Grand%20juror%20called%20case%20against%20Broadview%206%20a%20crock%20of%20s---&tpcc=cst_cm" target="_blank" >a “crock of sh--.”</a></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/06/09/broadview-six-grand-jury-midway-blitz-boutros-trump?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=061026%20Morning%20Edition&utm_content=061026%20Morning%20Edition+CID_e5cb798cbab6da1240e3e04b560963b8&utm_source=cst_campaign_monitor&utm_term=Grand%20juror%20called%20case%20against%20Broadview%206%20a%20crock%20of%20s---&tpcc=cst_cm" target="_blank" >Transcripts reveal tension, improprieties during ‘Broadview 6’ grand jury hearings</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The panelists did not reject every case brought by the feds. Rather, grand jurors in Chicago indicted<b> </b>14 of the Midway Blitz defendants. They include<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/02/03/marimar-martinez-shot-border-patrol-chicago-speaks-out-after-good-pretti-deaths-i-am-their-voice" target="_blank" >Marimar Martinez</a>, the woman whose shooting by a Border Patrol agent<b> </b>is now <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/08/25/marimar-martinez-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-chicago-police-cpd" target="_blank" >under investigation by the Chicago Police Department</a>.</p><p>Martinez’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/11/20/operation-midway-blitz-marimar-martinez-anthony-ruiz-us-supreme-court-feds-drop-case-against-woman-shot-by-border-patrol-agent-in-brighton-park" target="_blank" >charges were later dropped</a>. In fact, prosecutors secured convictions against only two of the 33 defendants, with one case still pending. U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros<b> </b>has said his office reviewed hundreds of potential cases and wound up declining many charges.</p><p>The new insight into grand jury proceedings became available Thursday through procedural records that were previously kept under seal because of the strict rules governing grand jury secrecy. They were filed after initial charges were brought against two Midway Blitz defendants: Sheridan and Nathan<b> </b>Griffin.</p><p>Prosecutors<b> </b>sought<b> </b>additional time<b> </b>to indict<b> </b>both of them last fall, and they justified their request in the sealed records. U.S. District Chief Judge Virginia Kendall, who supervises grand jury operations, approved each request.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> Federal Courthouse in October 2023.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Neither defendant was ever indicted, though. Grand jurors directly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/10/federal-grand-jury-rejects-another-midway-blitz-case-this-time-against-laugh-factory-manager" target="_blank" >rejected the effort to indict Griffin</a>, in a once-rare rebuke of prosecutors known as a no-bill. Chicago’s federal court has since adopted a rule requiring <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/18/department-of-justice-doj-federal-court-chicago-no-bill-grand-jury" target="_blank" >public disclosure<b> </b>of a no-bill</a><b> </b>under similar circumstances.</p><p>The feds’ struggle here and elsewhere put an unusual spotlight on an arm of the federal courts long viewed with cynicism. Generally made up of 16 to 23 people, grand juries operate behind closed doors and hear only from prosecutors and witnesses before deciding whether to indict. Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure forbid<b> </b>prosecutors, panelists<b> </b>and others<b> </b>from discussing the proceedings.</p><p>It’s long been said that prosecutors can convince grand jurors to indict a ham sandwich.</p><p>Boutros’ office did not object to the Sun-Times’ request to unseal the records, allowing the rare glimpse into the grand jurors’ response to Midway Blitz.</p><p>“Given the unique and intense interest in Operation Midway Blitz cases, the office elected not to oppose the request for disclosure of these sealed attachments so the public can see for themselves that the government’s handling of Midway Blitz cases was no different from how it handles federal criminal cases in this district,” Boutros’ office said in a statement.</p><p>Boutros spent his summer weathering a scandal directly tied to grand juries. A prosecutor from his office<b> </b>is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/05/21/broadview-ice-protest-grand-jury-transcript-kat-abughazaleh-trump" target="_blank" >accused of misconduct while securing an indictment</a> last fall against the group of Midway Blitz protesters known as the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/06/27/broadview-six-boutros-chicago" target="_blank" >“Broadview Six.”</a></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" He delivered the news to Kendall Thursday<b> </b>that Boutros’ office would not object to the Sun-Times’ request for the records.</p><p>The judge said she expected a different response from Boutros’ office. Though she granted the media organization’s request, she questioned whether the public’s interest in the records really outweighed the need for grand jury secrecy.</p><p>She told a Sun-Times lawyer, "it's not normally something that you are allowed to have.”</p><h3><b>Push for Bovino’s testimony</b></h3><p>Federal prosecutors<b> </b>filed<b> </b>an initial assault charge<b> </b>against Sheridan<b> </b>on Oct. 4, using a document known as a criminal complaint. That gave them until Nov. 3<b> </b>to secure an indictment over Sheridan’s run-in with Bovino.</p><p>The incident took place outside <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/10/01/broadview-immigration-processing-center-detention-ice-dhs" target="_blank" >an immigration holding facility</a><b> </b>in west-suburban Broadview that became a hotbed of protests during Midway Blitz.</p><p>Authorities did not use Bovino’s name in the criminal complaint. Rather, they identified him in a sealed filing Oct. 31, when they asked Kendall<b> </b>for<b> </b>five additional days to secure an indictment.</p><p>Sheridan has said Bovino lied about what happened.<b> </b>Reached Thursday by the Sun-Times, he compared his prosecution to the<b> </b>investigation of late<b> </b>financier<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/03/02/epstein-commission-illinois-bill-abdelnasser-rashid-kwame-raoul" target="_blank" >Jeffrey<b> </b>Epstein</a>, accused of sexually abusing underage girls.</p><p>“If you can, with absolutely no evidence, just send a random person to jail and potentially get an indictment out of it, then what can you do with, you know, a massive tranche of emails [and] documents,” Sheridan said. “That’s got no legs?”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Bears' rare 'diamond' Colston Loveland has the wedding invite to prove it
entries.summary: <p>If there’ were any doubt about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> tight end Colston Loveland’s place in the NFL landscape, consider this: he was invited to the wedding of the year.</p><p></p><p>Loveland attended Travis Kelce and global superstar Taylor Swift’s nuptials in Madison Square Garden on July 3, the result of the relationship he’d developed with the Chiefs star through the “Tight End U” offseason summit.</p><p></p><p>Loveland was the only <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/halas-intrigue/2026/09/01/bears-kyler-gordon-podcast-halas-intrigue" target="_blank" >Bears</a> player in attendance, though he had a few NFL friends there. The best part about the wedding, Loveland said, was people-watching. His favorite: actor and comedian Adam Sandler, who actually performed the ceremony.</p><p></p><p>“It was fun, man …” he told the Sun-Times with a smile breaking across his face. “A lot of elite people there. It was cool.”</p><p></p><p>Loveland may never reach the level of popularity of his new friend — and definitely not that of his singing sensation wife. In NFL circles, though, the second-year tight end is considered a budding superstar. And while attention is nothing new to the man from small-town Gooding, Idaho — he was the leading receiver in Michigan’s national championship game, after all —it’s reached a new level.</p><p></p><p>“I’ve been praying for times like this,” he said. “It’s very cool.”</p><p></p><p>It might be just the beginning for the someone who, at only 22, is already one of the league’s most unique weapons.</p><p></p><p>“Rare,” receiver Rome Odunze said. “A diamond.”</p><p></p><p>People Loveland’s size — he’s 6-6, 241 pounds, with huge 10-inch hands — don’t usually move the way he does. He’s fast, sure, but what impresses linebacker T.J. Edwards is how fluid he runs his routes. Most tight ends start chopping their feet when they’re getting ready to break out of their initial sprint, but Edwards can’t tell where Loveland is going to go.</p><p></p><p>He moves like a giant wide receiver, which is where the Bears put him last year. About 77% of his receiving yards came when he was either in the slot or split wide. He works on his craft like one, too, catching 100 balls from a JUGS machine— it’s a pitching machine for footballs — before every practice. He bought one for his house, too, and invites his teammates over on off days.</p><p></p><p>“That's the part that's gonna make him great,” receiver Kalif Raymond said, “because he wants it that bad.”</p><p></p><p>Loveland feels more confident than he did at this time last year, when he was learning the playbook after recovering from months-long shoulder surgery rehab. He’s found more efficient ways to go about his day, perfecting his note-taking in meetings, finding better stretching drills to do before practice and just learning how to manage his schedule while living on his own.</p><p></p><p>“It’s growing up,” he said.</p><p></p><p>The 10th pick of the 2025 draft led the Bears with 713 receiving yards last year. He averaged 1.9 yards per route run, the fourth-most of all qualifying tight ends.</p><p></p><p>He got better as the year went on. Over the Bears’ last five games, counting the postseason, he was targeted on 25% of the Bears’ passes and averaged 82 yards per game. Both would have led all NFL tight ends during the course of a full season.</p><p></p><p>Loveland is a willing blocker, too — “He’s holding his own like he's a tackle,” Odunze said — and that makes him the perfect Ben Johnson chess piece.</p><p></p><p>Last year, the Bears used two tight end sets 33% of the time, the sixth-most frequent in the NFL, and three tight ends 9% of the time, which was fifth.</p><p></p><p>At his core, Johnson lives to find advantages in the run game. He uses heavy formations to see how the opposing coordinator wants to counter the Bears. If the opponent uses five defensive backs, the Bears can lean on Loveland and Cole Kmet to block smaller players on run plays. If the opponent stays in base defense, Loveland will often end up being guarded by a safety or linebacker on passing downs.</p><p></p><p>“I think he’s a really hard matchup for any safety in this league, any linebacker in this league that wants to cover him in man,” Johnson said. “That’s a tough ask. He’s too big for these nickels to cover if that’s the matchup that ends up dictating itself.”</p><p></p><p>Which defender does Loveland prefer?</p><p></p><p>“I can’t tell on myself like that,” he said, laughing.</p><p></p><p>Kmet is curious what opposing coordinators will try against him.</p><p></p><p>“You for sure don't want the ‘backer on him, you don't want the safety,” Kmet said. “They go small on us, like, we're gonna run it down your throat. So you know he's definitely a weapon that opens up a lot of things for the offense.”</p><p></p><p>If Loveland gets double-teamed in the red zone, the Bears have plenty of options — receivers Rome Odunze and Luther Burden, running back D’Andre Swift, Kmet and others.</p><p></p><p>“We have so many other weapons,” Loveland said. “You can’t focus on one person or you’re going to get beat on the other side.”</p><p></p><p>Focusing on Loveland, though, would be a good place to start.</p><p></p><p>“He’s a huge asset for us,” Johnson said.</p>

entries.title: Mother charged with killing 2-year-old child in Frankfort before trying to harm herself
entries.summary: <p>A mother has been charged with murdering her 2-year-old child at a home in south suburban Frankfort, where authorities found the boy unresponsive and the mother trying to harm herself.</p><p>Corie A. Walsh, 40, remains held for medical treatment and, once released, will be transferred to Will County Jail to await a detention hearing on three counts of first-degree murder, Frankfort Police Chief Leanne Chelepis said in a news release.</p><p>"Our thoughts and prayers are with the family, their loved ones, and everyone affected by this heartbreaking tragedy," Chelepis said in the statement. "We ask our community to keep them in their thoughts and prayers and to respect their privacy as they navigate this profoundly difficult time."</p><p>Officers responded around 4 p.m. Tuesday to the home in the 22700 block of Brook Stone Court for a call of an unresponsive child, police have said. The boy was taken to a hospital and pronounced dead, police said. The Will County coroner's office said the death <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/02/2-year-old-child-killed-in-frankfort-home" target="_blank" >was an “apparent homicide,”</a> and has not released a cause or the boy's name.</p><p>Police said the child’s mother also was inside the home, police have said. She was trying to harm herself, and was taken to a hospital with injuries that were not life-threatening, police said.</p><p>At the time of the call, three other children were at the home unharmed, Chelepis said in Friday's statement.</p>

entries.title: White Sox activate starting catcher Kyle Teel off IL, option Drew Romo
entries.summary: <p>With 22 games left in their unlikely pursuit of an American League Central title, the White Sox are getting their starting catcher back.</p><p>Kyle Teel, limited to just 19 games this season due to a right hamstring strain, a right knee sprain and most recently, a left ankle sprain, was activated off the injured list ahead of Friday’s game against the Twins.</p><p>Drew Romo was optioned to Triple-A Charlotte to make room for Teel on the active roster, but will remain in Chicago with the team as a “taxi squad” player, ready to be activated if needed. Despite hitting .141/.239/.288 on the year, the 25-year-old Romo has appeared in 60 games this year <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/11/catcher-drew-romo-chicago-white-sox-anthony-kay-walker-mckinven" target="_blank" ><u>on the strength of his defense and pitching management</u></a>, with the Sox recently choosing to keep him over former top prospect Edgar Quero, who looks likely to finish the season with Triple-A Charlotte.</p><p>Recently acquired veteran backup Jake Rogers is just 4-for-30 at the plate since being picked up off waivers on Aug. 14. But he maintains a strong defensive reputation and as a career .216/.298/.452 hitter against left-handed pitching, Rogers is a more natural platoon partner for the left-handed hitting Teel, and will remain on the active roster. Joey Bart looked primed to assume temporary starting catcher duties when the White Sox acquired him from the Braves at the Aug. 3 trade deadline, but he remains sidelined by a fracture in his left hand caused by a hit-by-pitch suffered in just his third game with the club.</p><p>Not making his season debut until late June, Teel’s bat did not get going (.190/.271/.317) in the brief window he was active this season, and he struggled with blocking pitches on defense. But after he hit .273/.375/.411 as a 23-year-old in his rookie season last year, combined with the coaching staff’s view of his pitch-framing potential and Quero’s struggles on both sides of the ball, Teel’s place as the team’s long-term starting catcher has remained relatively stable.</p><p>At 73-67, the White Sox maintain a three-game lead in the AL Central despite receiving the least offensive contributions from the catching position to date (.529 OPS) of all 30 MLB teams.</p>

entries.title: Chicago murals: Roseland cop house mural features the neighborhood that teens want to see

cop house is an initiative from Ald. Anthony Beale (9th) to help deter crime in the Calumet District. “Cop” stands for community-oriented policing. The house, which is at 12020 S. Indiana Ave., is modeled after a program in Racine, Wisconsin, that places resource houses in high-crime neighborhoods. At the cop house, which is expected to open this fall, residents can get to know local law enforcement and tap community services, like workforce development training and job readiness programs. It also can serve as a gathering spot for the community or a quiet spot to stop and stay for a bit.</p><p>Most of the teens depicted in the Roseland mural were eighth graders last year.</p><p>“I’m an artist that really believes [in] real people, real stories,” says David Guana, the Pilsen-based artist who designed the mural. He spoke with the students and with community residents to find out what they wanted. What he heard was “more representation of people like themselves in public art. They wanted to see businesses.”</p><p>They "wanted the tone of the piece to be something positive, something prideful,” he says.</p><p>So, he worked with art teacher Nicolas Pesa to recruit the students to help him paint the mural. Their faces are on the mural. So is the face of a beloved former school security guard who recently died. Their images appear over a map of Roseland, with shoutouts to local businesses like Old Fashioned Donuts and Shorty’s Mexican Grill. Pesa pulled it together with colorful rainbow arcs of pink, yellow and green.</p><p>The group painted the mural with acrylic and spray paints before applying a protective coating and mounting it on the wall of the brick, two-story home.</p><p>Now, it sits on the north wall of the house.</p><p>Chicago Neighborhood Initiative is the nonprofit that owns the house and is developing the project. It also provided the grant for the mural, says senior project manager Donald Higgins.</p><p>In the end, Higgins says, the project is about the community.</p><p>“We’re partnering with the police and neighboring organizations to have this as a space where we can provide programming” like workforce development training, job readiness programs and trauma services. “It’s pretty much a resource for entries.title: CPS postpones Friday football games due to heat advisory
entries.summary: <p>Chicago Public schools has called off Friday's football games due to an excessive heat advisory in the city. </p><p>CPS postponed Thursday's games on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/03/cps-calls-off-thursday-football-games-due-to-heat" >Thursday morning</a> but then went ahead and played most games when the heat advisory was lifted later in the day. </p><p>Thirteen Public League football games were scheduled to be played in the city on Friday. Those are definitely postponed. </p><p>Simeon is scheduled to play at Morris and Morgan Park in Edwardsville. A CPS spokesperson is still confirming the status of those high profile away games. </p><p>Morgan Park coach Chris James confirmed he is expecting the Mustangs to play in Edwardsville on Friday.</p><h3>Friday’s postponed CPS football games</h3><p>Clark at Julian, 6</p><p>Comer vs. Ag. Science at Stagg Stadium, 4:30</p><p>Dunbar at ITW Speer, 6:30</p><p>Fenger vs. Chicago Richards at Eckersall, 4:30</p><p>Hyde Park vs. South Shore at Lane, 7:30</p><p>Lincoln Park vs. Curie at Rockne, 7:30</p><p>Mather vs. Sullivan at Lane, 4:30</p><p>Pritzker vs. DRW at Hanson, 4:30</p><p>Senn vs. Lake View at Winnemac, 4:30</p><p>Solorio at Chicago Academy, 3:45</p><p>UIC Prep at Rauner, 4:15</p><p>Vocational at Taft, 7</p><p>Von Steuben vs. Prosser at Hanson, 7:30</p>

entries.title: Man dies of heat-related causes on South Side, raising Cook County's heat death toll to 14
entries.summary: <p>A man died on the South Side this week due to heat-related causes, becoming the 14th person to die this year from high temperatures in Cook County.</p><p>Bill J. Humphrey, 78, died Wednesday night at a home in the 1700 block of East 86th Place in Avalon Park, according to the county's medical examiner's office. Autopsy results released Friday showed he died of heart disease with "heat stress" marked as a contributing factor.</p><p>Chicago police did not immediately share additional information.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-b00000" name="html-embed-module-b00000"></a><div style="min-height:897px" id="datawrapper-vis-yDuNX"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/yDuNX/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-yDuNX"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/yDuNX/full.png" alt="Heat-related causes have killed fourteen so far this year in Cook County, with eleven dead in Chicago (Locator map)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Eleven of the 14 heat-related deaths in Cook County have happened in Chicago. All 11 of those people have died on the South or West sides, except for one person who died on in the East Side neighborhood.</p><p>More people have died from the heat in Cook County this year than in any previous year of the last decade, according to a WBEZ and Chicago Sun-Times <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/30/extreme-heat-wave-death-chicago-cook-county-oak-lawn-july-stroke-stress-elderly-air-conditioning" target="_blank" >analysis</a>. For comparison, the previous two peak years topped out at six deaths each in 2019 and 2022.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-bd0000" name="html-embed-module-bd0000"></a><div style="min-height:544px" id="datawrapper-vis-Nexc6"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Nexc6/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-Nexc6"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Nexc6/full.png" alt="Fourteen people have died so far this year in Cook County from heat-related causes, the most in at least a decade (Column Chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>The Chicago area was under heat-related advisories for most the last week. On Wednesday, the day the latest heat-related death was recorded, a high temperature of 96 degrees was recorded at O'Hare Airport. High humidity has pushed the heat index, or how the temperature feels, past 100 degrees multiple times this week.</p>

entries.title: Construction to start soon at long vacant LeClaire Courts site on Southwest Side
entries.summary: <p>It’s been a long time coming, but work is expected to start soon on a large Southwest Side tract where the LeClaire Courts housing project once stood.</p><p>Developers plan an October groundbreaking for the first phase of a heavily subsidized complex of apartments, mostly for renters with low or moderate incomes. The design calls for two six-story buildings encompassing 183 units on busy Cicero Avenue just south of Interstate 55.</p><p>It’s the start of something more ambitious — maybe 700 homes in all — on a 32-acre site that has worried Garfield Ridge neighbors and puzzled passersby. The Chicago Housing Authority tore down decayed LeClaire Courts in 2011, leaving open land on a heavily traveled route from the highway to Midway Airport.</p><div class="Enhancement" entries.title: WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert will retire in December
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/wnba" >WNBA</a> Commissioner Cathy Engelbert is retiring at the end the year, bringing to a close her seven-plus years at the helm of the league and a stewardship that has been transformative and at times tumultuous.</p><p>Engelbert is the second-longest tenured WNBA president or commissioner, and she helped negotiate a lucrative collective bargaining agreement this past spring that resulted in the league's first set of million-dollar player salaries.</p><p>"Cathy has presided over the WNBA through the most significant period of growth in the league's 30-year history," NBA Commissioner Adam Silver said Friday when announcing Engelbert's decision. "We are grateful for Cathy's leadership and unwavering commitment to the advancement of women's basketball."</p><p>Engelbert, who turns 62 in November, told The Associated Press that she has been thinking about retiring for months.</p><p>"When I first came to the league I intended to do this for 3½ years," she said in a phone interview. "The 7½ years exceeded that time. This is a really good time given the financial transformation journey we've been on. Getting the collective bargaining agreement done, getting a long-term media rights deal done, getting expansion done."</p><p>Engelbert insists that the decision to leave was solely her own and that she did not feel any pressure to step down from NBA or WNBA stakeholders.</p><h3>Several unidentified successors on league’s radar</h3><p>The commissioner said she has been working on a succession plan over the last few years. While she didn't give any specifics on who might be considered for the position, Engelbert did say there are both internal and external potential candidates on the league's radar.</p><p>"It's a good time to hand it off to the next leader to take the 'W' into a better phase," she said. "I'm proud of the team we built and everything we accomplished. A leader knows when it's time to drop the mic and move on after building a powerhouse team in the league office."</p><p>Engelbert said she has mixed emotions about leaving.</p><p>"I love women's basketball and am not going anywhere yet. We'll run a real succession process in the remaining four months. If we don't find someone I'll stay on," she said. "I had no transition. I walked in the door and I was by myself as no one transitioned me into this role.</p><p>"Hopefully I can help this next leader transition in especially considering the elevation of this league."</p><p>The WNBA has grown at an exponential rate during Engelbert's tenure as commissioner, with record television ratings, strong attendance, a new long-term media rights deal and expansion to 18 teams by the end of the decade.</p><p>"I was brought in as a business leader to transform the business," she said. "I look at revenue and merchandise, viewership and attendance," she said, noting how they've all improved. "A great leader senses when it's time for someone else to come in. When I came in, this league was facing questions about our long-term viability and sustainability."</p><h3>Turmoil and tension part of Engelbert’s tenure</h3><p>Engelbert said the growth of the league has "blown away her expectations" since she stepped into her role after leaving her previous position as president of Deloitte in 2019.</p><p>Besides the new CBA, the list of things she is most proud of includes getting charter travel for players, keeping the league going during the coronavirus pandemic, the historic media rights deal and exponential increase in the value of of WNBA franchises. In 2019, the average value of a WNBA franchise was $10 million; in 2026, it is about $460 million.</p><p>Along with the financial gains, however, turmoil and tension have accompanied the WNBA's growth.</p><p>Players say they have seen more social media vitriol directed toward them over the last few years and some don't feel the league has done enough to ensure their safety. The league also has been at the center of discussions about transgender athletes playing in the league.</p><p>Engelbert has repeatedly said the online attacks of players are unacceptable and she backs league initiatives to protect players. She also said there should be no confusion on the transgender question.</p><p>"We have no current eligibility issues in the WNBA," Engelbert said, adding that "if we did, we would have a thoughtful policy discussion with the (players' association) and the players."</p><p>While there was a strained partnership between the commissioner and players during the recent CBA negotiations, Engelbert insists she has a good relationship with them.</p><p>New York Liberty forward Breanna Stewart, vice president of the WNBA players' union executive committee said Friday that she was happy for Engelbert.</p><p>"What she's done for the league is incredible," Stewart said. "Obviously, the CBA negotiation was a tough one, but the way that both sides continue to have a huge win is really important. So really happy for her and hope that she continues to remember that and reflect on that."</p><p>Stewart had said before the All-Star Game in July that there was a respect for Engelbert among the players but not much of a relationship.</p><p>Engelbert sent a letter to all the players Friday morning in which she wrote that she had "enormous pride in what we've accomplished together, profound gratitude for the opportunity to lead alongside of you, and complete confidence that the future of the WNBA is brighter than ever."</p><h3>What’s next in Engelbert’s future?</h3><p>Engelbert said she is ready to do what most retirees plan: spend more time with family.</p><p>She also admitted that the online hate she receives has affected her family as well, though she did not share details of the impact.</p><p>"There have been some hard parts of that on my family with the vitriol and hate I get online," Engelbert said.</p><p>Her retirement will make her mother happy.</p><p>"My mom is turning 90 this year, and she said that 'it would be good if you were retired to spend more time with me,'" Engelbert said, laughing. "I have two children, one I barely see.</p><p>"I'm one of eight kids (and I) have five brothers. They always say can you retire so you can spend more time with us."</p><p>Come Jan. 1, her family will get its wish.</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: Enes Kanter Freedom responds to stadium ban by suing the Sky
entries.summary: <p>You haven’t heard the last from Enes Kanter Freedom.</p><p>After the former NBA player was ejected and banned from a Sky game during which he got into a verbal altercation with Natasha Cloud, he is now suing the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> and the City of Chicago for conspiring to violate his First Amendment rights.</p><p>Kanter Freedom has been using the WNBA in recent months to draw attention to his view that transgender women should be barred from women’s sports. He went as far as to mock the league and the queer community by claiming to be a woman and declaring for the 2027 WNBA draft.</p><p>Kanter claims he was ejected and banned for wearing a shirt that read, “WOMAN noun, adult human female." Sky principal owner Michael Alter had previously said that Kanter was ejected because security determined he was a potential threat during his altercation with Cloud.</p><p>Kanter Freedom's lawsuit presents him as a victim of an unfair double standard. The complaint says that Cloud was triggered by his T-shirt and launched a “profanity-laced” tirade without being ejected. Meanwhile, Kanter Freedom claims he was ejected for peacefully demonstrating his First Amendment rights and, as he puts it, “protecting women’s sports."</p><p>When asked about the altercation last week, Cloud called Kanter Freedom “irrelevant” and then redirected the conversation to issues women actually need to be protected from, like domestic violence and sexual abuse.</p><p>A statement Friday from Alter called the lawsuit “meritless” and “frivolous.”</p><p>“Freedom’s claim that he was removed from Wintrust Arena due to this speech is false. As his own complaint acknowledges, he wore the shirt in question for multiple hours without any contact with security. Security removed Freedom only after he violated a code of conduct by rising from his seat, gesturing at a player, and stepping toward the court.”</p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module entries.title: Illinois joins lawsuit against latest Trump admin push to cut funding for youth gender-affirming care
entries.summary: <p>Illinois is suing the Trump administration, along with more than 21 legal officials from states and cities nationwide, over its attempts to barrel through a ban on gender affirming care for youth — despite another federal court striking down its last attempt earlier this year.</p><p>In March, Oregon District Court judge Mustafa Kasubhai sided with Attorney General Kwame Raoul and others in <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/transgender-health-care-lawsuit-ruling-robert-kennedy-25adf96f745c5364c2ebf8c3f27cab71" target="_blank" ><u>striking down</u></a> a near-identical rule change from Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.</p><p>In a social media post Tuesday, Trump said he instructed the Administrator of the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services and former television personality Mehmet Oz to push the nearly identical rule through his agency.</p><p>The new policy calls for Medicaid and CHIP to continue to pay for mental health treatment for transgender patients 19 and younger but phase out coverage of hormone treatments as of April 2027. If courts don’t intervene, the new rule could go into effect Oct. 13.</p><p>The states now argue in Massachusetts federal court that Oz, much like Kennedy, is circumventing the usual legal methods for the rule changes in an attempt to create a near-nationwide ban on gender-affirming care for patients under 18. The action also threatens Children’s Health Insurance Program, or CHIP, funding if it’s used to provide the care to 19-year-olds, who are legal adults.</p><p>The lawsuit says the move “excludes medically necessary healthcare services from federal reimbursement only when provided to low-income transgender adolescents” while flying in the face of how Medicare and Medicaid exclusions have traditionally been set — by the states.</p><p>In a statement, Raoul said not only was the rule targeting transgender youth, but that it could open the door for the federal government to make more decisions about practiced medicine.</p><p>“The Trump administration is attempting to score political points by continuing to threaten healthcare for a very small and vulnerable population,” Raoul said. “No federal agency has the power to directly regulate the practice of medicine. … If the Trump administration is allowed to decide what is safe and appropriate healthcare for this population, what’s to stop them from meddling in everyone’s care?”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2025/12/24/illinois-joins-suit-trump-administrations-attempted-nationwide-ban-on-gender-affirming-care-for-youth" >Illinois joins lawsuit against White House’s attempted national ban on youth gender-affirming care</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/lgbtq/2025/08/01/illinois-sues-the-trump-administration-to-protect-access-to-gender-affirming-care" >Illinois sues the Trump administration to protect access to gender-affirming care</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/06/22/federal-trade-commission-world-professional-association-transgender-health" >Federal Trade Commission sues Chicago-area transgender health group</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Raoul and the coalition of legal officials made <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2025/12/24/illinois-joins-suit-trump-administrations-attempted-nationwide-ban-on-gender-affirming-care-for-youth" target="_blank" ><u>nearly identical arguments in the previous suit</u></a>, also saying Kennedy’s move violated the federal Administrative Procedures Act. In his decision, Kasubhai chastised the federal government for its attempt to circumvent federal checks and balances.</p><p>“The notion that ‘I will go forward and issue a declaration and see if we can get away with it’ is not a principle of governance that adheres to the overarching commitment to a democratic republic that requires the rule of law to be regarded and respected and honored as a sacred,” Kasubhai said in his ruling.</p><p>It comes months after the Department of Justice issued more than 20 subpoenas for patient data regarding gender-affirming care and the Federal Trade Commission <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/06/22/federal-trade-commission-world-professional-association-transgender-health" >sued the East Dundee-based World Professional Association for Transgender Health</a>, accusing it of making deceptive claims.</p><p>The Trump administration's actions run counter to the recommendations of major U.S. medical societies such as the <a class="Link" href="https://pediatrics.aappublications.org/content/142/4/e20182162" target="_blank" ><u>American Academy of Pediatrics</u></a> and the <a class="Link" href="https://policysearch.ama-assn.org/policyfinder/detail/%22Clarification%20of%20Evidence-Based%20Gender-Affirming%20Care%22?uri=%2FAMADoc%2FHOD-185.927.xml" target="_blank" ><u>American Medical Association</u></a>. But many hospitals across the nation, including in the Chicago area, have <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2025/07/29/chicago-hospitals-are-scaling-back-trans-care-for-youth-a-rapid-response-team-is-stepping-in" target="_blank" ><u>cut treatment for thousands of patients</u></a> out of fear of reprisals from the federal government.</p><p>Earlier this year, Illinois joined a third separate lawsuit with more than a dozen other attorneys general alleging the Trump administration <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/lgbtq/2025/08/01/illinois-sues-the-trump-administration-to-protect-access-to-gender-affirming-care" target="_blank" ><u>overstepped its authority by threatening health care providers</u></a> with federal investigations and criminal prosecutions.</p><p><i>Contributing: AP</i></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/06/16/school-districts-trans-kids-pay-anti-trans-lawsuits" >School districts, trans kids pay for anti-trans lawsuits cropping up across U.S.</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/06/30/supreme-court-says-states-can-ban-trans-girls-from-playing-womens-sports" >Illinois affirms trans girls can play on girls’ sports teams, as Supreme Court upholds state bans</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/06/01/state-lawmakers-laud-passage-of-bills-protecting-reproductive-gender-affirming-care" >State lawmakers laud passage of bills protecting reproductive, gender-affirming care</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Have you been swarmed by biting flies? Why they're 'no joke'
entries.summary: <p>From Rogers Park to Calumet, many people in the Chicago area are reporting a surge in flies.</p><p><b>Are there more flies, especially ones that bite?</b></p><p>The public health departments of Chicago and Illinois don’t track biting flies. But anecdotally, they seem ubiquitous. Social media is buzzing with people lamenting getting attacked by flies everywhere from Belmont Harbor to Logan Square.</p><p>“Today at a park in West Town I got swarmed by like seven flies after sitting on the ground for less than five minutes with my dog. Those bites are no joke,” wrote one Reddit user this week.</p><p>Another Reddit user had to leave Oak Street Beach, “because there were hundreds of flies that kept landing on me and staying on my skin. Felt like tiny needles. I’ve never experienced this at the beach.”</p><p>Lifeguards at lakefront beaches have been spotted wielding flyswatters and flies are swarming dogs on walks.</p><p><b>Why are there more flies?</b></p><p>Very wet and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/09/01/september-october-chicago-heat-wave-is-this-normal" target="_blank" ><u>hot weather</u></a> in recent months could be a factor.</p><p>This summer, the Chicago area has seen some of the most <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/14/chicago-area-under-flood-watch-friday-night-through-saturday-morning" target="_blank" ><u>severe storms</u></a> in recent years. It has also been very hot, with several <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/09/01/september-october-chicago-heat-wave-is-this-normal" target="_blank" ><u>heat waves</u></a>.</p><p>Wet and warm conditions are typically good for breeding insects. But Nina Salem, founder of the Insect Asylum in Avondale, said favorable weather conditions vary for different species.</p><p>Yet Salem noted that she and other wildlife rehabilitators have been seeing a big uptick of “fly strikes.” That’s when flies lay eggs on animals such as squirrels and raccoons. After hatching, flies burrow into animals, alive and dead.</p><p>Salem cautioned against washing any affected animals because water will trigger hatching of eggs, which look like white rice.</p><p><b>What kind of flies are we likely seeing? </b></p><p>There are many kinds of biting flies, according to the <a class="Link" href="https://dph.illinois.gov/topics-services/environmental-health-protection/structural-pest-control/biting-flies.html" target="_blank" ><u>Illinois Department of Public Health</u></a>.</p><p>But the stable fly is a likely culprit because they peak in late summer and early fall. It’s gray with four dark stripes behind the head. This bloodsucker “will fly several miles to bite livestock (hence the name), pets and people,” said the department’s website. “They typically bite in early morning or late afternoon and often attack the ankles, inflicting a sharp, stabbing pain.”</p><p>Stable fly larvae “live in and eat decaying vegetation that washes up along the shore,” according to the <a class="Link" href="https://www.nps.gov/piro/planyourvisit/insects.htm?fbclid=IwY2xjawUH3qlwZG9mBWV4dG4DYWVtAjEwAGJyaWQRMU1Cc3llYmI1eGNSOFQ3emFzcnRjBmFwcF9pZBAyMjIwMzkxNzg4MjAwODkyAAEerYLCiCHpRQ5C5qu-N1XnczRjkAZrZMpzyKDbxDnXIYz7WX-6-70vb1_TQ44_aem_mJvCRaold8J2_yP2tIggBQ" target="_blank" ><u>National Park Service</u></a> in Michigan’s Pictured Rocks. They don’t transmit disease to humans, but “are annoying enough to drive people away from beaches.”</p><p>Stable fly outbreaks have occurred along the shores of Lake Michigan, Chris Stone, medical entomologist at University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, wrote in an email. “This species is considered to be more abundant in years with high rainfall. So a peak this year would make some sense,” he said.</p><p>Other biting flies include deer flies, which are most abundant in the spring, as well as horse flies. Some horse flies are entirely black, while “greenheads” are light brown with shiny green eyes. Larvae live in water or moist locations.</p><p><b>Are fly bites especially painful?</b></p><p>They can be.</p><p>Stable flies suck blood through a pointed proboscis. “They have bayonet-like mouthparts with rasping teeth at the tip that they use to cut through or abrade the skin to create a pool of blood on which they feed,” Stone explained..</p><p>Deer and horse flies bite with “scissor-like mouthparts that cut into skin, causing blood flow which the flies lap up,” according to the Illinois Department of Public Health. This crude blood sucking can be especially painful.</p><p><b>What are officials doing about the flies?</b></p><p>Chicago Parks District “has not received an influx of concerns regarding the presence of biting flies, mosquitos and other insects in our parks,” Michele Lemons, director of communications, wrote in an email.</p><p>The parks department hasn’t seen park use drop. “In fact, for many of our programs, we saw an increase in participation this summer,” said Lemons.</p><p>But on Friday morning, <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/lfparksandrec?__cft__[0]=AZhDcdSG8DeQ6phyV_TZEX8t66jpYq1JKPBzz_-N-mvwmc2g7KbOPwA0TYWTBM-M9NVnOut-x9HMsHc8BbjWvBXmRcGHbJ7A_QJfkzbq4n16kHOFBaQYhcb06UspnnduhB8NvHSqYvH_9Cpo0CmJoks4vQ8eZ2xq&__tn__=-UC%2CP-R" target="_blank" >Lake Forest Parks and Recreation</a> department treated Forest Park Beach with an “EPA-approved product.”</p><p>The department said on <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/lfparksandrec/posts/pfbid06SgbUA59sH1CXtqtmn5piYeZGFUKFY3JzFmKvpURdU9qPTsFBvDM7nz6tjgZQwmVl" target="_blank" ><u>Facebook</u></a>, “While we can all agree our beach is amazing, the latest increase in fly activity is not!”</p><p>Indiana Dunes National Park warned about an outbreak of biting flies on Facebook, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.audacy.com/wbbm780/news/local/biting-flies-are-swarming-indiana-dunes-beachgoers" target="_blank" >WBBM News Radio</a> in Indiana. Park staff noticed a surge in biting flies on some eastern beaches about a week ago. </p><p>On Thursday, the Illinois Department of Public Health said it’s working on updating guidelines on managing flies and bites.</p><p><b>What can I do?</b></p><p>Most insect repellent doesn’t work on stable flies. Since they target legs and ankles, the <a class="Link" href="https://www.nps.gov/piro/planyourvisit/insects.htm?fbclid=IwY2xjawUH3qlwZG9mBWV4dG4DYWVtAjEwAGJyaWQRMU1Cc3llYmI1eGNSOFQ3emFzcnRjBmFwcF9pZBAyMjIwMzkxNzg4MjAwODkyAAEerYLCiCHpRQ5C5qu-N1XnczRjkAZrZMpzyKDbxDnXIYz7WX-6-70vb1_TQ44_aem_mJvCRaold8J2_yP2tIggBQ" target="_blank" ><u>National Park Service</u></a> recommended wearing long pants and socks – not ideal for the beach.</p><p>In any case, stable flies can pierce through clothing, according to fly control company <a class="Link" href="https://info.spalding-labs.com/biting-stable-flies/" target="_blank" ><u>Spalding Labs</u></a>.</p><p>Salem noted that parasitic wasps can eat flies. But if fly predators aren’t handy, she and Stone suggested treating clothes with permethrin, a chemical insecticide.</p><p><b>How long will this last?</b></p><p>A stable fly’s <a class="Link" href="https://extension.okstate.edu/programs/livestock-entomology/stable-flies" target="_blank" ><u>life span</u></a> is 20 to 30 days. In the U.S, their peak season is July through September. But they can remain into October in warmer regions.</p><p>This summer, the Chicago area has endured heat waves, tornadoes, rainstorms, wildfire smoke and deafening <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/cicadas-louder-mating-brood-decibels-coping-mechanisms-dog-days-summer-heat-trees" target="_blank" ><u>cicada</u></a> choruses. Now it’s biting flies. What’s next?<br></p>

entries.title: In Dansby Swanson’s absence, Nico Hoerner slides over to short and reminds everyone he’s a Gold Glover, too
entries.summary: <p>When Dansby Swanson <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/17/cubs-injuries-dansby-swanson-oblique-edward-cabrera-blister-nico-hoerner-pedro-ramizrez-craig-counsell-david-peterson-javier-assad-rotation-bullpen" target="_blank" >went down with a strained oblique</a>, it fell to Nico Hoerner to man shortstop and keep the Cubs’ best-in-baseball defense churning without one of its top contributors.</p><p>But, hey, remember that Hoerner is a two-time Gold Glover, too.</p><p>Hoerner won those awards in 2023 and 2025 as the Cubs’ everyday second baseman. Swanson has collected the same hardware in 2022 with the Braves and 2023 with the Cubs.</p><p>But Hoerner’s no stranger to short, having played it coming up through the minors and even for an entire big-league season the year before the Cubs signed Swanson.</p><p>If that experience wasn’t recent enough for you, however, then you’ll just have to check the video.</p><p>Hoerner is one of those defensive dudes, no matter where he’s playing, and he delivered one of the highlights of the season with a jaw-dropping catch Wednesday against the Brewers.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Nico Hoerner WHAT A CATCH 😱 <a href="https://t.co/UnEYJCWDXd">pic.twitter.com/UnEYJCWDXd</a></p>— MLB (@MLB) <a href="https://x.com/MLB/status/2095325793333178445?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">September 3, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>‘‘Does it surprise anybody?’’ Swanson said Friday. ‘‘Of course, he’s going to make [the catch]. He’s so good at whatever he does, really. I’ve had zero doubts that this would be any different.’’</p><p>That’s the theme of the Cubs’ responses when they’ve been asked about Hoerner’s temporary move to short.</p><p>That it’s a talking point at all is a testament to the sort of difference-maker Swanson has been. Former Padres manager Mike Shildt said Swanson ‘‘almost single-handedly beat us with his glove’’ <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2025/10/02/cubs-playoffs-dansby-swanson-defense-wild-card-padres-nico-hoerner-mike-shildt" target="_blank" >in the National League wild-card series last season</a>.</p><p>But while the Cubs are at their best defensively with Swanson at short, there seemingly has been little drop-off with Hoerner there.</p><p>They haven’t slowed down as far and away the best defensive team in the majors, starting Friday leading baseball in defensive runs saved (105; next-best is 75), outs above average (63; next-best is 38) and fielding run value (64; next-best is 33.3).</p><p>‘‘It doesn’t really feel like much is really different,’’ center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong said Thursday. ‘‘No shade to Dansby. Nico’s showing everybody that he can be a big-league shortstop at the everyday clip, as well. Nico’s been nails.’’</p><p>‘‘If there’s another guy in this league I want playing shortstop, it’s Nico Hoerner, so there’s not much to complain about with that,’’ first baseman Michael Busch said late last month. ‘‘Dansby has shown what he’s capable of, taking over a game. To be honest, I don’t think we’re missing much.’’</p><p>They’re not missing nothing, of course, and Swanson’s value goes beyond what he does in the field.</p><p>Not only does he still rank fifth on the team with 18 home runs, despite being out since mid-August, but he has been described as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/18/dansby-swansons-presence-will-be-part-of-cubs-efforts-to-weather-his-absence-he-turns-into-another-coach" target="_blank" >someone who makes those unquantifiable contributions</a> to a championship-caliber group.</p><p>‘‘One thing that Dansby does, in the clubhouse and in the locker room, his presence carries weight,’’ Busch said during a road trip on which Swanson stayed back to work in Chicago. ‘‘He’s one of the best teammates I’ve ever been around, thinking about himself, thinking about others, thinking about the game, thinking about how to win. He thinks about all those things at a different level from a lot of guys.</p><p>‘‘The locker-room presence is one thing you kind of miss with him [not here].’’</p><p>The Cubs aren’t just good at defense; they’re built around it. And the double-play combo of Swanson and Hoerner, which has logged so much time together since Swanson arrived in 2023, is as good as it gets.</p><p>‘‘When you play with someone long enough, there almost becomes this unsaid communication,’’ Swanson said. ‘‘Me and Nico don’t even have to really say it; we just kind of look at each and just give a signal, and we know.’’</p><p>There has been an understandable learning curve with Hoerner and rookie Pedro Ramirez, who has taken over second-base duties and has been praised all season for being mature beyond his years.</p><p>But the defense hasn’t stopped humming.</p><p>The Cubs can thank Hoerner, who has made the loss of their starting shortstop in the middle of a playoff race not as big a deal as it might have been.</p><p>‘‘Nico’s really good over there,’’ left fielder Ian Happ said late last month. ‘‘We have all the confidence in the world that Nico can play shortstop.</p><p>‘‘We’re pretty lucky, as a team, to have that as the backup option.’’</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" entries.title: Kyle Teel is back for the White Sox, and they need him to hit and stay healthy
entries.summary: <p>Catcher <b>Kyle Teel </b>has been here before. Not just with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a>, but answering questions about coming back from an injury.</p><p>“I’m very excited. Going into this interview, I was like it’s going to be a lot of the same questions,” Teel said. “Yeah, I’m just ready to get going.”</p><p>The Sox desperately need that to be true.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/04/white-sox-activate-starting-catcher-kyle-teel-off-il-option-drew-romo-edgar-quer-joey-bart-jake-rogers" >Activated from the injured list</a> before Friday’s game against the Twins, Teel could finally give the Sox some offensive production from behind the plate. Entering the game, Sox catchers were slashing a ghastly.170/.258/.270, and Teel figures to improve on those numbers.</p><p>If he stays healthy.</p><p>Because of a hamstring strain, knee sprain and the ankle sprain he came back from, Friday was Teel’s 20th game. Despite that, Teel is not thinking about whether he can trust his body.</p><p>“I’m not going out there to make sure I’m OK,” Teel said. “I’m going out there to win.”</p><p>To make room for Teel, the Sox optioned <b>Drew Romo</b> to Triple-A Charlotte. Romo, however, is staying with the Sox on their taxi squad.</p><h3>The Castillo question</h3><p>Through six starts, <b>Luis Castillo</b> has a 7.52 ERA, a 1.709 WHIP and given up at least four runs in five outings. Castillo, who will get $22.75 million from the Sox next year before a 2028 vesting option, also isn’t giving the Sox any length as only one of his starts has lasted more than five innings.</p><p>General manager <b>Chris Getz</b> wondered whether Castillo is trying too hard to impress in his new surroundings. He also said the Sox are making tweaks with Castillo’s mechanics, and they saw progress with his lower half Thursday in Houston.</p><p>“He’s not exactly where we want him to be or showing what he’s capable of doing, but that doesn’t mean we don’t continue to work,” Getz said. “That’s kind of the beauty of what we do and what we’ve done. We’ll continue to do so, find ways to solve for problems and issues and make adjustments.”</p><p></p><h3>Wave the wand</h3><p>He hasn’t thrown a pitch this year, but the story of the 2026 Sox won’t be told without pitcher <b>Mike Vasil</b>. Out for the season with Tommy John surgery, Vasil has stayed with the team and become one of its most noticeable fans, waving a “magic” wand and putting a wizard’s hat on teammates when they hit a home run.</p><p>On Friday, the Sox gave away souvenir wands to the first 20,000 fans, which is quite a statement about a player who won’t return until 2027.</p><p>“He’s a guy that when he comes into the clubhouse, whether he has a story for you or just his presence and general positivity and energy makes you forget about yesterday and helps you focus on the task at hand tonight,” manager <b>Will Venable</b> said. “He’s made a huge impact.”</p><p></p><h3><b>Mark your calendars?</b></h3><h3></h3><p>The Sox announced their 2027 spring training schedule, which is slated to begin Feb. 19 with a game at the Dodgers. Two days later, the Sox are scheduled to host the Reds for their spring home opener.</p><p>This is all pending the labor situation and the collective bargaining agreement, which expires Dec.
